# Introduction to QA Testing
## Concepts Software Development Software Development Life Cycle Requirement Gathering and Analysis Planning Design Development Software Testing Deployment Maintenance Quality Assurance
## Introduction Software has become an integral part of our daily lives, from the apps on our smartphones to the programs we use on our computers and the systems that operate our cars. Millions of users are relying on software applications, making it crucial to ensure that they function correctly and meet user needs. This is where QA Testing plays a vital role. Before diving into the world of QA Testing, it's important to have a basic understanding of software development and the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). So far we have learned to write code/programs for defined inputs and expected outputs. In this unit, we will learn about software development and the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). We will explore the different stages of software development and understand how the software is created.
## 1. Software Development Software Development is the process of planning, designing, documenting, coding, testing, and bug fixing involved in creating and maintaining applications. **Coding vs Software Development** Coding refers to the act of writing and implementing code using programming languages to create software applications. On the other hand software development involves various tasks like planning, designing, testing, and fixing issues in addition to coding. It takes a comprehensive approach to create and maintain applications, focusing not only on writing code but also on other important aspects of the process. Developing the softwares requires proper planning, design, development, etc. This structured process is commonly known as Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC).
## 2. Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) The Software Development Life Cycle is a methodology with clearly defined processes to produce high-quality software that meets or exceeds customer expectations. SDLC is an important process for developing and delivering software products. The SDLC includes different phases that are designed to ensure the quality and efficiency of the software product. The different phases of SDLC are:
Consider we got a requirement of developing an E-Commerce application similar to Amazon. Now, let’s understand how can each phase helps us develop this E-Commerce application. ### 2.1 Requirement Gathering and Analysis This phase involves gathering, documenting, and managing the requirements and analyzing them for feasibility. The purpose of requirement analysis is to make sure that the software system fulfills the requirements of the users and other involved parties. Let's see the requirements of an E-Commerce application. #### E-Commerce Application - Requirements Below are sample requirements that should be considered for an E-Commerce application: - User sign in/sign up - Shopping Cart - Payment Gateway - Shipping - Logout etc. #### Analyzing the Requirements It involves identifying dependencies and determining the feasibility of implementing the requirements within the project constraints. | Requiremet | Dependency | | :-----------------------: | :-------------------------------------------------: | | For User Sign in/Sign up | Having a user database | | For Shipping Requirements | Collaborating with shipping service providers, etc. | #### Outcome In the requirement analysis phase, the outcome is the creation of the Software Requirements Specification (SRS). The SRS serves as a blueprint during the design and development stages of a software engineering project. A well-defined description of the software requirements will guide the development team throughout the project. ### 2.2 Planning
In the planning phase, the project team creates a plan that outlines the project's scope, timeline, and resources, based on the gathered requirements. In this phase, the project team creates a plan that outlines the following project parameters: - **Scope:** This involves determining what will be included and excluded in the software product's current version, such as features and functionalities. - **Deadlines and Effort:** This includes creating realistic timelines and budget estimations for the completion of each phase of the project. - **Resources:** This involves identifying the required team members, hardware, software, and other tools needed to successfully complete the project. #### E-Commerce Application - Planning | Parameter | E- Commerce Explanation | | :------------------: | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Scope |
  • Including features like user registration and login, shopping cart functionality, etc.
  • Excluding features like recommendation system
| | Deadlines and Effort |     Planning for a timeline of, say, 6 months and respective budget | | Resources |
  • Team Members: UX/UI designers, frontend & backend developers, database administrators, testers, etc.
  • Tools: Development platforms, database systems, testing tools, etc.
| #### Outcome The outcome of the planning phase of SDLC is an achievable project development plan that includes detailed schedules, cost estimations, and procurement requirements. ### 2.3 Design In this phase, the project team creates the overall architecture and user interface of the application based on the gathered requirements. For Example: - User Interface - Database Tables, etc. #### E-Commerce Application - Design **User Interface**
**Database Schema and relationships between them**
#### Outcome The outcome of the design phase is a comprehensive Software Design Document(SDD) that is prepared as per the Requirement Specification Document (RSD). The SDD describes the architecture, design, and implementation of the software system. It is a critical document that is used by the development team to build the software system. ### 2.4 Development In the development phase, developers perform the following tasks: - Writing Code based on design Specifications - Developing Databases based on schema - Developing user interface based on designs #### Outcome The outcome of the development phase is a version of the software that can be tested. ### 2.5 Software Testing
In this phase, software testers perform various tests to validate the software and identify defects and bugs based on the requirements document. By identifying and resolving problems, testing plays a vital role in improving the overall quality of the product. In the software testing phase, the testing process evolves through different stages: 1. **Debugging**: This involves identifying and fixing errors or defects in the software. 2. **Positive Testing**: Tests are conducted to demonstrate that the software works as intended, meeting the specified requirements. 3. **Negative Testing**: Tests are designed to intentionally break the software and identify areas where it doesn't work as expected or handle invalid inputs. 4. **Risk-based Testing**: Tests focus on reducing risks by targeting critical areas or functionalities that have a higher probability of failure or impact. Each phase builds upon the previous one, gradually improving the quality and reliability of the software through a systematic testing approach. #### Examples of Software Bugs/Defects **Bug in the pricing functionality**: The customer added two Items to the cart, but charged for three.
The expected total in the cart is 2 x 200 = 400. But the actual price for the product in the cart is 600. This shows an example of a bug in the pricing functionality. #### Outcome The outcome of the software testing phase is to ensure that the software is ready for release. This means that the software has undergone thorough testing, defects have been identified and addressed, and it meets the specified requirements. ### 2.6 Deployment
In this phase, the final product is delivered to end-users by making it available for download, access, or installation. Some of the tasks involved in the deployment phase include: - **Physical environment (Hardware)**: Setting up the necessary hardware infrastructure required for the software application. - **Documentation**: Preparing comprehensive documentation to guide users and system administrators. - **Setting up links**: Configuring web links to make the application accessible to users over the internet. - **Setting up a database**: Configuring and populating the database with real user data to simulate real-world usage scenarios. #### Outcome The outcome of the deployment phase is to have a stable and operational environment ready to host and serve the software to end users, ensuring that the software goes live and is accessible to its intended users. ### 2.7 Maintenance The application has been deployed and is being used by millions of users. So we need to maintain servers. In this phase, the software is released to the users, and any issues/defects that arise are addressed and fixed by the development team. In the Maintenance phase, the following things should be considered: - Gather feedback from users to identify areas of improvement in the application. - Maintain the software by fixing bugs and updating to ensure smooth operation. - Continuously improve the application by adding new features and many more. Maintenance activities can be categorized into the following types: - Adaptive maintenance - Corrective maintenance - Perfective maintenance - Preventive maintenance **2.7.1 Adaptive Maintenance** - Adaptive Maintenance involves making modifications to the software to ensure its compatibility with changes in the application's environment, such as hardware or software upgrades, operating system updates, or new regulatory requirements. - It doesn't involve fixing any fundamental flaws or errors in the system itself. Instead, the focus is on adapting the software to meet new requirements and external factors without altering its core functionality. #### Example: An example of adaptive maintenance is Amazon incorporates a new UPI payments feature to accommodate the growing demand for convenient payment options. This adaptive maintenance allows Amazon to stay competitive in the market and provide its customers with a convenient and widely used payment option. **2.7.2 Corrective Maintenance** Corrective maintenance refers to the process of addressing and fixing defects, bugs, or issues identified in a software system after it has been deployed. This type of maintenance is typically triggered by user reports, error logs, or monitoring tools that detect abnormal behavior or malfunctions in the software. #### Example: An example of corrective maintenance is when a user reports a bug in an E-Commerce website where the checkout process fails to complete the transaction. Similarly, a bug in the pricing functionality example in the Software Bugs/Defects section also falls under corrective maintenance. **2.7.3 Perfective Maintenance** Perfective maintenance involves making enhancements and improvements to the software system to optimize its performance, usability, and functionality. It focuses on adding new features and improving existing features. It is the system upgrade kind of work that makes the system work more efficiently. #### Example: An example of perfective maintenance is when a social media platform introduces a new feature that allows users to schedule posts in advance. This enhancement improves the user experience by providing a convenient and time-saving functionality. **2.7.4 Preventive Maintenance** Preventive maintenance involves activities aimed at proactively addressing potential issues and improving the long-term stability and maintainability of a software system. It focuses on preventing future problems and optimizing the system's performance. #### Example: A real-time example of preventive maintenance is the installation of operating system (OS) security updates. OS vendors regularly release updates to address known vulnerabilities, improve system performance, and enhance overall security. After the software development life cycle (SDLC) is complete, the software is ready to be delivered to users. However, it is important to remember that software can still have issues even after it has been through a rigorous testing process. So, maintenance is a continuous process and involves continuous monitoring and management of the application to identify and address any issues, make necessary improvements, and adapt to changing user needs and technological advancements. ### Issues One common issue that software can experience is high traffic(a large number of users are trying to access the website). During high-traffic events, such as big billion days or festival sales, the website experiences a slowdown or even gets crashed. This is an issue that might not be identified during normal software testing but could be a critical problem in a real-world scenario. Before delivering software to the client, it's essential to verify that it is of high quality and meets all the client's requirements.
## 3. Quality Assurance Quality Assurance is a process that ensures that the software meets the necessary requirements and quality standards (like functionality, performance, scalability, etc.) | Attribute | Description | | :-----------: | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------: | | Functionality | The software should be able to perform all the functions and operations specified in the requirements document | | Scalability | The software should be able to handle increasing amounts of traffic without significant drops in performance | | Performance | The software should operate smoothly and quickly, without lagging or crashing during high volumes of traffic | Quality assurance is involved in every phase of the software development life cycle. #### Quality Assurance - Requirement Gathering & Analysis Quality Assurance in Requirement Gathering & Analysis aims to make sure that the requirements are clear, accurate, and free from any confusion or mistakes. For example, if the requirement document does not include necessary payment options like UPI. Customers may shop on other platforms that provide these payment options, causing lost sales and revenue. Here, quality assurance involves reviewing and verifying the requirements to ensure accuracy and on-time completion. It helps in identifying any potential issues.
### Summary - Software Development: Creating and maintaining software applications. - Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC): Methodology with clearly defined processes to produce high-quality software. It consists of phases like requirement gathering, planning, design, development, testing, deployment, and maintenance. - Requirement Gathering & Analysis: gathering, documenting, and managing the requirements and analyzing them for feasibility. - Planning: Creating a plan that outlines the project's scope, timeline, and resources. - Design: Creating the architecture and user interface of the software. - Development: Writing code, developing database, and developing user interface. - Software Testing: Performing various tests to validate the software and identify defects and bugs. - Deployment: Making the software available to end-users for download, access, or installation. - Maintenance: Addressing issues and continuously improving the software. - Quality Assurance: Ensuring software meets requirements and quality standards.

# Understanding Testing Fundamentals - Part 1
## Concepts Software Testing Basic Terminology Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC) Requirement Analysis Planning Test Case Development Test Environment Setup Test Execution Test Cycle Closure SDLC vs STLC
## Introduction In the previous unit, we understood each phase of the software development life cycle. In this unit, we will learn key aspects of software testing such as the Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC), important terminology including issue, bug, and defect, and essential testing components such as test cases, test suites, and test plans, which are vital for ensuring software quality and reliability.
## 1. Software Testing We know that software testing is the evaluation process to check if a software product meets requirements and is free of defects/bugs. Let's get to know the importance of software testing. ### Importance of Software Testing
As humans, we are prone to making mistakes, and even the most skilled individuals can overlook errors that may have an impact on the outcome. The following are key points highlighting the importance of software testing: - Software Testing helps us to identify errors, gaps or deviations from actual requirements in the given software. For example, if an online shopping website has a defect that prevents us from adding items to their cart or completing a purchase, testing can help identify this issue. - Testing helps to ensure that the software is of good quality. It helps to identify any issues with the software, such as crashes or performance problems. For example, if an application we are using frequently crashes or takes an unreasonably long time to load, it can be identified and resolved through testing. - Testing helps to ensure that the software meets the needs and expectations of the user. For example, if a new feature is added to a software application, testing can help ensure that it functions as expected and meets the needs of the user before it is released. - Testing helps to catch mistakes early on in the development process. Fixing these mistakes early is much less expensive than waiting to fix them later. For example, if a bank's mobile app allows others to access our account information, this could result in a costly breach of security. Testing can help identify and fix this mistake before the app is released, avoiding potential financial and reputational damage to the bank. ### Software Bugs/Failures Software bugs could be expensive or even dangerous and can potentially cause monetary and human loss. **Examples:** #### 1. Expensive Accident In April of 1999, a software bug caused the failure of a $1.2 billion military satellite launch, the costliest accident in history. #### 2. Monetary Loss Some of Amazon’s third-party retailers saw their product prices reduced to 1 paisa due to a software glitch. They were left with heavy losses. #### 3. Human Loss In 1994, in Scotland, a Chinook helicopter crashed, causing the tragic loss of all 29 passengers. An investigation later revealed that a systems error, specifically a software issue, played a significant role in the crash. The above incidents remind us of the serious outcomes that can happen due to software bugs. They show us the critical importance of carefully testing and ensuring the quality of critical systems during their development. Before delivering software to the client, it's essential to verify that it is of high quality and meets all the client's requirements.
## 2. Basic Terminology In software testing, there are a few key terms that it are important to understand. These terms include: - **Issue** - **Bug** - **Defect** - **Test Plan** - **Test Case** - **Test Suite** ### 2.1 Issue Issue refers to any problem, error, or flaw encountered during SDLC. It can also include performance problems, usability concerns, or even missing features. For example, let's say we're using an online shopping website, and the product pages take a really long time to load, we can consider it as an issue. ### 2.2 Bug The Bug is a specific type of issue caused by a coding error or mistake in the software. Bugs affect the functionality or behavior of the application. For example, If we are unable to add items to the shopping cart due to an error in the code, it would be considered a bug. Bugs need to be fixed by the development team to ensure the software functions correctly. ### 2.3 Defect Defect is another term for a bug or flaw in the software that deviates from its intended functionality. Any issue that can be found after the application goes into production is referred as a defect. For example, let's imagine we are trying to make a payment online, but the system fails to process our transaction correctly. In such a situation, we would consider it a defect in the application. In the field of software testing, the terminologies such as **issue**, **defect** and **bug** are used interchangeably. ### 2.4 Test Plan A Test Plan in software testing is a document that outlines: - Scope of testing - Testing strategies - Estimated effort - Costs for testing and many more. #### Test Plan Document | Parameters | Example | | :--------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Scope of Testing | The features of the application:
Login functionality, Search functionality, etc | | Testing Strategy/Methodology | Methods/techniques to be used:
Functionality Testing, Performance Testing, etc | | Resource Allocation | Resources to be involved in testing:
Testers, Developers, etc | | Testing Schedule/Timeframe | The timeline for testing | ### 2.5 Test Case A test case is a specific set of conditions, inputs, and expected outcomes designed to verify the functionality of a software system or component. Each test case has an expected outcome, and if the software behaves as expected, then the test case passes. If not, it fails. There are certain standard fields that need to be considered while preparing a Test case template. Some of the major fields are as follows: - **Test Case Id** Test Case Id: Test case identifier that provides information about the type of test and its sequence. _Example:_ TC\_FUNC\_3 indicates Functional Test Case - 3. - **Short Description** Short Description: A concise summary that describes the specific aspect being tested. _Example:_ Verify the functionality of the "Add to Cart" button. - **Description** Detailed explanation of the test case, including the objective and expected outcome. _Example:_ This test case aims to validate the functionality of the "Add to Cart" button on the product details page. It ensures that clicking the button adds the item to the user's shopping cart successfully. - **Pre-requisites** Any necessary conditions or actions that need to be met before executing the test case. _Example:_ The user should be logged in and have access to the product details page. - **Test Steps** Sequential instructions outlining the steps to be followed during the execution of the test case. _Example:_ - Open the application. - Log in with valid credentials. - Navigate to the product details page. - **Test Data** Input data or values required for the test case execution. _Example:_ Product information, such as product ID, name, and price, to be used for testing. - **Status** The current status or result of the test case, typically marked as Pass, Fail, or In Progress. _Example:_ Pass (if the "Add to Cart" functionality works correctly) or Fail (if the item is not added to the cart as expected). - **Remarks** Additional comments, observations, or notes related to the test case execution. _Example:_ The *Add to Cart* functionality was tested successfully, and the item was successfully added to the shopping cart. #### Sample Test Case | Scenario | Test Case | Test Steps | Test Data | Expected Result | Actual Outcome | Status | | :-----------------------: | :--------------------------------------------------: | :-------------------------------------------------: | :------------------------------------: | :----------------------: | :--------------: | :----: | | Check login functionality | Check response on entering valid username & password | Enter username
Enter password
Click Ok button | Username: rahul
Password: rahul123 | Login must be successful | Login successful | pass | ### 2.6 Test Suite A Test Suite in software testing is a collection of test cases that are intended to test a specific behavior of the software application. A Test Suite can include multiple test cases for a particular feature or multiple features of the application. A Test Suite helps testers organize and manage the testing process efficiently. _Example:_ #### Shopping Cart Test Suite
Similar to the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC), the Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC) is a structured approach followed by testing teams to ensure thorough and effective testing of software applications. Within the SDLC, the software testing phase is where the STLC comes into play. The STLC focuses specifically on the testing activities within the larger SDLC framework. It outlines the different stages and activities involved in testing the software for defects and ensuring its quality. Let us know the Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC) and its phases.
## 3. Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC) The software testing life cycle (STLC) is a systematic approach to testing software applications. It consists of several phases that ensure comprehensive testing. STLC is conducted in the Testing phase of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC). It focuses on verifying and validating the software to ensure it meets the intended requirements and functions correctly. Similar to SDLC, STLC also consists of multiple phases, where each phase involves specific tasks to be carried out ### 3.1 Requirement Analysis In this phase, the test team studies/analyzes Requirements Specification Document (RSD) to identify whether the requirements can be tested or not #### Example #### Outcome The outcome of this phase is the list of all testable requirements. If the testing team encounters any non-testable requirements, they will communicate it to respective stakeholders (product owner, etc) and get them clarified. ### 3.2 Planning In this phase, a Test Plan document is created by the Test Lead which outlines the: - Scope - Effort - Cost Estimates for the Testing It includes details like what will be tested, how it will be tested, who will do the testing, and when the testing will take place. #### Example For example, we will conduct functionality testing and performance testing for the login functionality and search functionality over a period of two weeks, involving both testers and developers. #### Outcome The outcome of this phase is Test Plan Document. Sample Test Plan Document: | Parameters | Example | | :--------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Scope of Testing | The features of the application:
Login functionality, Search functionality, etc | | Testing Strategy/Methodology | Methods/techniques to be used:
Functionality Testing, Performance Testing, etc | | Resource Allocation | Resources to be involved in testing:
Testers, Developers, etc | | Testing Schedule/Timeframe | The timeline for testing | ### 3.3 Test Case Development In this phase, the testing team writes the test cases to test the software. They also collect test data for testing. Test Data is the data used as input for testing a software application. #### Example Sample Test Case: | Scenario | Test Case | Test Steps | Test Data | Expected Result | Actual Outcome | Status | | :------------: | :-------------------------------------------: | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------: | :-------------------------: | :---------------------------------------: | :---------------------------------------: | :----: | | Product Search | Verify that the user can search for a product | 1. Log in to app
2. Enter a product name in the search bar
3. Click Ok button | Product Name: Running Shoes | List of products matching the search text | List of products matching the search text | pass | ### 3.4 Test Environment Setup This phase involves setting up the test environment with the necessary hardware, software and network configurations. #### Example #### Outcome The outcome of this phase is a properly configured test environment that closely resembles the production environment where the software will be deployed. This allows us to perform accurate and reliable testing to identify any issues or bugs before the software is released to users. ### 3.5 Test Execution In this phase, the testers execute the Test Cases. They compare the expected results with the actual results and also log effects/discrepancies if found during testing. If a test case result is Pass/Fail then the same should be updated in the test cases. The defect report should be prepared for failed test cases and reported through a bug-tracking tool for fixing the defects. ### 3.6 Test Cycle Closure In this phase, a document that gives a summary of all the tests conducted during the STLC will be prepared The development team then addresses the bugs mentioned in summary by modifying the source code or making configuration changes. After bug fixes, the software undergoes retesting within the STLC to ensure the successful resolution of the identified issues. It also gives a detailed analysis of the bugs removed and errors found for every cycle. ### 4. SDLC vs STLC - SDLC focuses on the overall software development process, including requirements gathering, design, development, testing, deployment, and maintenance. - STLC is a subset of SDLC that specifically focuses on the testing activities involved in ensuring the quality of the software being developed. - SDLC is a broader framework that encompasses the entire software development process, while STLC is specifically concerned with testing activities and processes.
### Summary - Software Testing: - Evaluating software to ensure it meets requirements and functions correctly. - Identifying defects and errors in the software. - - Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC): - Requirement Analysis: Understanding and analyzing software requirements. - Planning: Developing a test plan. - Test Case Development: Creating detailed test cases. - Test Environment Setup: Setting up necessary resources. - Test Execution: Running test cases and comparing actual results with expected results. - Test Cycle Closure: Analyzing results, preparing reports, and obtaining feedback. - SDLC focuses on the overall software development process, while STLC focuses on testing activities.

# Understanding Testing Fundamentals Part - 2
## Concepts Types of Testing Functional Testing Non-Functional Testing Testing Techniques Black Box Testing White Box Testing Grey Box Testing Testing Approaches Manual Testing Automated Testing
## Introduction In the previous unit, we understood each phase of the software testing life cycle. In this unit, we will learn about manual testing and automated testing, understand the various testing techniques and approaches, and familiarize ourselves with different types of testing.
## 1. Types of Testing We know that software testing is the process of ensuring that a software application is working correctly. During each phase of the STLC, we need to perform different types of testing to ensure the software meets the specified requirements. Software testing is the process of ensuring that a software application is working correctly. There are different testing types to software testing depending on the objective of the testing. Let's explore the various types of software testing to gain a better understanding of their purposes and methodologies. ### 1.1 Functional Testing It is a type of software testing which is used to verify the functionality of the software application. **Example** It involves checking different functionalities of the website like: - Are we able to browse the catalog of items? - Are we able to add items to the shopping cart? - Are we able to remove items from the shopping cart? - Are we able to checkout and pay for the items? There are four most common types of functional testing: #### 1.1.1 Unit Testing It involves testing individual parts, or "units", of the software application. This could be testing a single function or module of code. #### Example Let's say, we have a function that calculates the square of a number in our code. During unit testing, we aim to verify whether the code accurately calculates the square or not. #### 1.1.2 Integration Testing It is a type of software testing in which individual software modules are combined and tested as a group to evaluate the interactions and data exchange between those components. #### Example
Here, we have an example of integration testing where we combine two test cases to test the functionality of adding products to the shopping cart and calculating the total price: Test Case 1: Add Products to the Shopping Cart. - Add a product with a price of 100 to the shopping cart. - Verify that the product is successfully added. Test Case 2: Calculate Total Price - Add another product with a price of 50 to the shopping cart. - Calculate the total price. - Verify that the total price is 150. Here, we do integration testing by verifying that products are added correctly to the shopping cart, and the total price calculation provides the expected output. #### 1.1.3 System Testing System testing is a level of software testing that focuses on evaluating the entire system as a whole. #### Example 1. Test Case 1: User Registration - Register for a user account. - Verify that the user is logged successfully. 2. Test Case 2: Product Listing - Browse the product listing. - Verify that all products are correctly displayed with accurate details. 3. Test Case 3: Shopping Cart - Add products to the shopping cart. - Verify that the selected products are added correctly and the total price is calculated accurately. 4. Test Case 4: Payment Processing - Proceed to checkout and select a payment method - Simulate a payment transaction using a test payment gateway - Verify that the payment is processed successfully and the order is confirmed Here, we do system testing where we test the overall functionality of the system that allows users to sign in/sign up, displays available products, stores selected products, calculates the total price, and handles payment processing. #### 1.1.4 Acceptance Testing It aims to verify whether a system meets the specified requirements and is suitable for delivery to the end-users or stakeholders. #### Example Testing For example, let's imagine we are testing an E-Commerce website where users can browse and purchase products. During acceptance testing, we would perform tasks such as: - Creating a new user account and verifying that the registration process is smooth and error-free. - Browsing through different product categories, adding items to the shopping cart, and ensuring that the website accurately reflects the selected products. - Proceeding to the checkout process, entering shipping and payment details, and verifying that the transaction is processed correctly. - Testing various payment methods, such as credit cards or digital wallets, to ensure they function as expected. - Verifying that order confirmations and email notifications are sent promptly to users after successful purchases. - Testing the website's responsiveness and compatibility across different devices and web browsers to ensure a consistent user experience. - Checking if the website adheres to any specific design or branding guidelines, ensuring it represents the business appropriately. Now, let's learn about non-functional testing, which involves testing software for factors other than just its basic functions. ### 1.2 Non - Functional Testing It evaluates important aspects of the software beyond its functional behavior, such as performance, security, usability, and other requirements. #### Example Let's say we're testing an e-commerce website that has thousands of users logging in at the same time In non-functional testing, we would test the website's performance under heavy load to ensure that it doesn't crash or slow down. There are four most common types of non-functional testing: #### 1.2.1 Performance Testing It ensure that a software program or system achieves specific performance objectives, such as desired response time. #### Example We test the website's speed when you click on categories or search. The test ensures fast response and quick display of results. #### 1.2.2 Security Testing Security testing involves assessing the website's protection against unauthorized access and potential security vulnerabilities. #### Example - We test the website's login feature to ensure it securely prevents access with incorrect passwords. - We test whether the website implements secure connections (HTTPS) to protect users' data, especially when handling sensitive information like payment details. #### 1.2.3. Load Testing Load testing involves evaluating the website's performance under high user traffic. #### Example We have a website that is used by millions of people every day. During high-traffic events, such as Big billion days, our website can experience slowdown or even crash. To prevent this, we perform load testing on our website before these events. The load test ensures website stability under increased traffic, checking for crashes or significant slowdowns. #### 1.2.4 Usability Testing Usability testing assesses the website's user-friendliness and ease of navigation. #### Example We verify if the website has user-friendly menus, buttons, and search functions, which ensures easy navigation and a smooth purchasing process. ### More Testing Types In addition to these software testing types, there are also other types of testing that are important while performing software testing. They are - Regression Testing - API Testing #### Regression Testing Regression testing is performed to ensure that recent changes or updates in the software do not negatively impact previously working functionalities. ### Example We make changes to the website's checkout process by adding a new payment method. To ensure that this change does not introduce any issues in existing functionalities, we conduct regression testing. We verify that all previously working features, such as adding items to the cart and applying discount codes, still function correctly after the update. #### API Testing API testing involves testing the application programming interfaces (APIs) to ensure they function correctly, securely, and efficiently. #### Example We have an e-commerce application that interacts with a UPI (Unified Payments Interface) application through an API integration. We conduct API testing to validate that the E-Commerce application can correctly send payment requests to the UPI application, receive payment confirmations, and handle any errors that may occur during the process. We have learned the different types of software testing, let's take a look at some of the testing techniques that can be used to perform these tests.
## 2. Testing Techniques Testing techniques are the methods used to evaluate software to find defects. There are many different testing techniques, each with its own purpose and benefits. Some of the most common testing techniques are as follows: ### 2.1 Black Box Testing It is a type of testing where the tester doesn't have any knowledge of the internal workings of the software. It focuses on examining the software's inputs and outputs without considering the internal code or structure. #### Example
In black box testing, we would test how the website behaves when a customer enters their personal information and clicks the "submit" button ### 2.2 White Box Testing White box testing is a type of testing where the tester has knowledge of the internal structure and code of the software. It involves testing the internal logic of the software. Testers use this knowledge to design test cases that ensure all parts of the code are tested thoroughly. #### Example Testing the checkout process of an online store. - Test Case 1: We verify that the shopping cart calculates the correct total price by checking the underlying code that performs the calculation. - Test Case 2: We test the handling of discount codes by examining the code logic that applies discounts and ensure that the correct discounts are applied. - Test Case 3: We validate the database updates by checking the code that updates inventory quantities after a successful purchase to ensure that stock levels are updated correctly. - Test Case 4: We test the error handling by intentionally triggering an error in the payment processing code and verifying that our system handles the error gracefully and displays an appropriate error message. - Test Case 5: We validate the integration with third-party payment gateways by examining the code responsible for communicating with the payment gateway API and ensuring that payments are processed correctly. ### 2.3 Grey Box Testing The tester has partial access to the internal workings of the software application. This approach combines elements of both black box and white box testing. #### Example In grey box testing, we might have access to the code that calculates the total cost of a customer's order, but not the code that handles the website's security
## 3. Testing Approaches Testing approaches are different ways or methods used to test software. These approaches determine how testing is carried out and can be broadly classified into two categories: ### 3.1 Manual Testing Manual testing involves human testers who carefully execute test cases and evaluate the software's functionality, usability, and other aspects. #### Example Imagine we are testers and using an e-commerce website to purchase a item. We should manually perform the following steps: - Open the website and search for the desired item. - Click on the item’s link to view its details. - Add the item to the shopping cart. - Proceed to the checkout page, enter the shipping address, and select a payment method. - Click the "Place Order" button to complete the purchase. As a tester we should follow the predefined set of steps, carefully observing and noting any issues, such as - broken links, - incorrect information, or - unexpected behavior, etc. ### 3.2 Automated Testing Automated testing involves using software tools and scripts to perform tests, eliminating the need for manual execution. It is more efficient and can quickly execute repetitive and complex test cases. Automated testing requires testers to write scripts or use testing tools to define the test scenarios and expected outcomes #### Example Imagine a software program that automatically interacts with the e-commerce website to simulate user actions: - The program searches for a specific product using predefined criteria. - It verifies if the search results match the expected outcome. - The program adds the product to the cart, simulating a user action. - It proceeds through the checkout process, entering predefined shipping and payment details. #### Manual vs Automation Testing | Manual Testing | Automation Testing | | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------: | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------: | | Testing performed by human testers manually executing test cases | Testing performed by using specialized software tools to execute test cases | | Test cases are executed manually, step-by-step, by following predefined procedures | Test cases are executed automatically by running scripts or test automation frameworks | | Time-consuming for large or complex applications | Faster execution and can handle large volumes of test data |
### Summary - Types of Testing: - Functional Testing: Verifying the functionality of the software application. - Unit Testing: Testing individual parts or units of the software. - Integration Testing: Testing the interaction and data exchange between software modules. - System Testing: Evaluating the entire system as a whole. - Acceptance Testing: Verifying whether the system meets specified requirements. - Non-Functional Testing: Evaluating aspects beyond functionality, such as performance, security, and usability. - Performance Testing: Checking if the software meets performance objectives. - Security Testing: Assessing protection against unauthorized access and security vulnerabilities. - Load Testing: Evaluating performance under high user traffic. - Usability Testing: Assessing user-friendliness and ease of navigation. - More Testing Types: - Regression Testing: Ensuring recent changes do not impact previously working functionalities. - API Testing: Testing application programming interfaces for correct functionality. - Testing Techniques: - Black Box Testing: Testing based on inputs and outputs without knowledge of internal workings. - White Box Testing: Testing with knowledge of internal structure and code. - Grey Box Testing: Partial knowledge of internal workings combined with black and white box testing. - Testing Approaches: - Manual Testing: Human testers execute test cases to evaluate functionality, usability, etc. - Automated Testing: Software tools and scripts are used to execute tests, improving efficiency.

# Getting Started with Selenium
## Concepts Automation Testing Selenium Automation Testing with Selenium & Java Installing IDE Installing Java (JDK) Installing Browser Driver Setting up the Selenium Project First Selenium Test using Java
## Introduction In the previous unit, we discussed various types of testing, including functional testing and non-functional testing. We explored different testing techniques such as black box testing, white box testing, and grey box testing. We also covered testing approaches, including manual testing and automated testing. Assume, we have an E-commerce application and we need to test it. To conduct manual testing, we will initially open the application in a web browser and then proceed to navigate through its various sections and features. Manual testing involves human testers who carefully evaluate the software's functionality. In automation testing, testers perform the exact same steps used in manual testing, but with the assistance of a tool In this unit, we will learn more about automation testing and a testing tool called Selenium.
## 1. Automation Testing We know that automation testing is one of the software testing approaches that involves using software tools and scripts to perform tests. It is more efficient and can quickly execute repetitive and complex test cases. **What can we automate?**
Automation Testing can be applied to various testing types including: - Unit Testing - Integration Testing - Regression Testing, etc Automation testing requires testers to write scripts or use testing tools to test the software. There are many tools available for automation testing. ### 1.1 Automation Testing Tools Some of the important tools of automation testing are as follows: - Selenium - Watir - QTP - Telerik Studio - Testim We will be using Selenium as it is an open-source and most commonly used automation testing tool.
## 2. Selenium Selenium allows us to validate web applications across different browsers and platforms with the help of test scripts. Test scripts: Instructions/code written to automate the testing process **Advantages of Selenium** Selenium is a highly flexible tool that supports a wide range of browsers, platforms, and programming languages It also supports all major operating systems like macOS, Windows, Linux, etc - **Open Source**: Selenium is an open-source tool, which means it is freely available and can be customized according to specific testing needs. - **Multiple Operating Systems**: Selenium supports multiple operating systems such as Windows, macOS, and Linux, allowing testers to perform cross-platform testing. - **Multiple Frameworks**: Selenium can be integrated with various testing frameworks such as TestNG and JUnit, enabling testers to utilize different testing techniques and functionalities. - **Multiple Browsers**: Selenium supports major web browsers like Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge, allowing testers to execute tests across different browsers to ensure compatibility. - **Multiple Programming Languages**: Selenium supports multiple programming languages such as Java, C#, Python, and JavaScript, giving testers flexibility in choosing their preferred language for test automation. ### 2.1 Suite of Software
Selenium Software is not just a single tool but a suite of software, each piece catering to different Selenium QA testing needs of an organization. Selenium is composed of several key components that work together to facilitate web automation testing. Components of Selenium - Selenium IDE(Integrated Development Environment) - Selenium Grid - WebDriver **2.1.1 Selenium IDE** It is the simplest tool in the suite of selenium. It is a browser add-on that helps us to create tests quickly through its record-and-playback functionality. It is mainly used for prototyping and not for creating automation in real-time projects. **2.1.2 Selenium Grid**
Selenium Grid is a component of the Selenium testing framework. It helps us in executing tests in parallel across different browsers, operating systems, and machines. It is used to run multiple test scripts on multiple machines at the same time. It helps in achieving parallel execution. #### Example Sometimes we may need to test our e-commerce application across multiple browsers and operating systems simultaneously. Selenium Grid helps in identifying any compatibility issues that may arise across different environments (different operating systems, and different browsers). **2.1.3 Selenium Web Driver**
Selenium WebDriver is a software library that programmers use to control web browsers and automate tasks on websites. It supports different programming languages and allows us to write the tests in our own choice of language. It interacts with the web browser using browser-specific drivers provided by the corresponding browser vendor. All these components can be either used individually or can be paired with one another to achieve a level of test automation. Now that we have learned about the different components and advantages of Selenium, let's explore how we can use Selenium and Java for Automation Testing.
## 3. Automation Testing with Selenium & Java Selenium supports multiple programming languages for automation testing In this course, we will learn to write Selenium tests using Java which is the most popular language. Java is considered one of the best languages for working with Selenium. It is widely used, has excellent support for Selenium, provides a rich set of libraries and frameworks, and offers good community support. Additionally, Java's object-oriented programming features make it suitable for building robust and maintainable automation frameworks. Before we start writing our first selenium test, we need to install a few prerequisites in our system: - Install IDE - Install Java (JDK) - Install Browser Driver Below are the required system configurations to run the selenium tests using Java. | System Configuration | Requirement | | :------------------: | :-------------------------------------------------: | | Operating System | 64-bit operating system | | Processor | Intel Core i5 / i7 or Higher | | RAM | 8 GB or Higher | | Disk Space | Minimum of 5 GB of free disk space for installation | ### 3.1 Installing IDE There are several popular IDEs (Integrated Development Environments) that are commonly used for Selenium automation testing. Some of the popular IDEs for working with Selenium include: Among the above IDEs IntelliJ IDEA is a popular Integrated Development Environment (IDE) that is widely used for Java projects. IntelliJ IDEA is a popular choice for Java development because it offers many helpful features, makes writing code easier, works well with other tools, and provides good support for testing. It also has additional features and options through plugins that can be added.
**3.1.1 Install IntelliJ on Windows**
Follow the below steps to download & install IntelliJ: - Click here and download the IntelliJ 2018.3.6 Version. - We choose to download the community edition of IntelliJ because it is available free of charge. - Scroll down the page and download the 2018.3.6 version for Windows - We download a file that is specific to our operating system because different operating systems have different file types. - Double-click on the downloaded file to run the executable file. - Follow the below steps to install IntelliJ. - Launch IntelliJ IDEA.
**3.1.2 Install IntelliJ on Ubuntu** - Open the `Ubuntu Software` application. - Click on the search button. - Now search "intellij" and select the `IDEA Community`. - Click on the snapstore to select the IntelliJ version - Scroll down and select the 2018.3.6 version. - Click on the `Install` button to install IntelliJ.
We have completed installing IntelliJ. Now let's install Java(JDK). ### 3.2 Installing Java (JDK)
**3.2.1 Installing Java on Windows**
Follow the below steps to install Java on Windows. - Click here to navigate to the download page. Scroll down and download **JDK11.x** for Windows which is one of the most compatible versions for Selenium. - Extract OpenJDK 11 Zipped Folder. - Configure OpenJDK 11 We need to configure Java on Windows by setting a Path environment variable. - Navigate to the **bin** folder within the extracted directory and copy the path of the **bin** folder. - Search for "Environment Variables" in the "Startup" menu. - Open the "Edit the system environment variables". - Click on the "Environment Variables" button. - Go to the "System variables" panel. Select the "Path" option and hit the "Edit" button. - Create a new variable and add the path of the **bin** folder we have copied. - Go to the "User variables" panel. Click the "New" button. - Navigate to the **jdk-11.0.2** folder within the extracted directory and copy the path of the **jdk-11.0.2** folder. - Add `JAVA_HOME` as the variable name and add the path of **jdk-11.0.2** as the variable value. - Open a new command prompt window and type `java -version`. It will display the version if we have successfully installed JDK.
**3.2.2 Installing Java on Ubuntu** Follow the below steps to install Java on Ubuntu. - Open the terminal - Enter the following command to install OpenJDK 11. ```xml sudo apt install openjdk-11-jdk ``` - Type **y** and hit Enter. - Open a new terminal and type `java -version`, it will display the version if we have successfully installed JDK.
After successfully installing OpenJDK 11, we will proceed to install the Chrome browser driver, which allows us to access Chrome using Selenium and Java. ### 3.3 Installing Browser Driver WebDriver interacts with the web browser using browser-specific drivers provided by the corresponding browser vendor. #### 3.3.1 Browser Drivers | Browser | Download Link | | :------------: | :-------------------------------------------------------------------: | | Chrome | http://chromedriver.chromium.org/downloads | | Firefox | https://github.com/mozilla/geckodriver/releases | | Opera | https://github.com/operasoftware/operachromiumdriver/releases | | Microsoft Edge | https://developer.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-edge/tools/webdriver/ | In this session, we would be performing the Selenium Java test on the Chrome browser #### 3.3.2 Downloading ChromeDriver To download the ChromeDriver follow the below steps: - Open http://chromedriver.chromium.org/downloads. - Check the current version of Chrome by following the steps below. - Download the suitable ChromeDriver for the current version of Chrome. - Download the Chrome driver. - Extract ChromeDriver Zipped Folder. We have installed all the necessary tools for our Selenium project. Now, let's begin our first project with Selenium.
## 4. Setting up the Selenium Project There are two common approaches to create a Selenium project: - Using Maven - Using plain Java We will be using Maven to create our Selenium project. ### Using Maven Maven is a widely-used build tool for Java projects that manages dependencies and automates tasks like downloading them, compiling code, running tests, packaging the project, etc. #### Maven Dependencies Maven dependencies are additional resources that a project needs to work properly. They are specified in a configuration file(**pom.xml**) and automatically downloaded by Maven. Dependencies help manage and integrate external libraries, plugins, or APIs into the project. Maven dependencies facilitate the management and integration of third-party libraries into a project, ensuring the availability of all necessary components during development and execution. Follow the below steps to set up the selenium project using Maven: - Create the Project in IntelliJ - Add Selenium WebDriver ### 4.1 Creating The Project Follow the below steps to set up the selenium project using Maven: - Create the Project in IntelliJ - Add Selenium WebDriver #### 4.1.1 Create the Project in IntelliJ Follow the below steps to create the selenium project in IntelliJ. 1. Let's search for IntelliJ in the "Start" menu and open it. 2. Accept the terms and conditions if shown. 3. Select the theme and click on "Skip Remaining and Set Defaults". 4. Now we click on the "Create New Project" button. 5. We select Maven for creating a maven project. 6. Now, click on "New" and Select "JDK" from the location where we have downloaded it. 7. Click on "Next". 8. Let's add the specified project configuration details as mentioned below. Here, - GroupId: `org.example` - ArtifactId: `first-test` It is a good practice to use the hyphenated-case for writing the articfactId where each word is separated by hyphens ("-"). Here, - Project name: `FirstTest` - Project location: `Choose the project location` 9. We have successfully created the project in IntelliJ. - Now, click on the "Maven" tab and check if all the required plugins are downloaded properly or not. If not downloaded, it will show the errors. - To resolve the issue, navigate to `Users -> -> .m2` and delete the `.m2` folder. - Now, click on the "Maven" tab and reload the project. Now, no errors should be shown. Let us look at the Maven project structure. **4.1.1 Project components** #### 1. Project Structure - In this project, we will find a directory structure, build and server configuration files, and a testing environment. - These components make our development organized, efficient, and error-free. #### 2. The `pom.xml` file - The `pom.xml` file contains information about the project and configuration details used by Maven to build the project. - The file uses XML language, a markup language like HTML. - The `pom.xml` configuration file is used to add project dependencies. #### 3. The `src` Folder Structure - The imageSrc folder is vital in the project structure and contains the code that defines the application's functionality. - It typically consists of "main" and "test" directories, with the main directory containing the source code and the test directory dedicated to unit tests, enabling effective development and testing processes. We will be using the **test** directory as we are going to test the web pages. #### 4. The `test` Directory - The test folders in Selenium projects typically contain test scripts, test data, test configurations, test fixtures, test reports, and test suites. - These elements are used to automate web application testing and organize test cases. ### 4.2 Integrating WebDriver To integrate WebDriver into our project, we need to add a specific dependency that provides the necessary libraries and functionality for interacting with web browsers programmatically. To get the selenium dependency we follow the below steps. - Open https://mvnrepository.com/ **MVN(Maven)** repository is a centralized source of software artifacts, making it easier for developers to manage dependencies and build their projects. - Search Selenium Java and click on it. - Click on the latest version 4.9.1. - Copy the code. - Now we add it in the `pom.xml` file between ` add here` tags. The `selenium-java` dependency provides support for Selenium WebDriver, which is the main component used for browser automation. After adding new dependencies to a Maven project, we need to reload the project to reflect the changes. We click on the "Maven" tab and select the reload icon to apply changes We added the required dependencies for our project. Let's begin by writing our first test case to validate the functionality of the web page.
## 5. First Selenium Test Using Java Let's write a test case to Open Flipkart, and get the webpage title. #### What to achieve? Open Flipkart, and get the webpage title using Selenium in Java. Below is the sequence of actions we may perform manually: 1. Open the application in the browser 2. Enter the Flipkart URL 3. Check the Application Title Manual testing involves human testers who carefully evaluate the software's functionality by following a sequence of steps Before writing any test case, it is essential to have a clear understanding of the test scenario. This helps us in defining the purpose and scope of the test, enabling us to design effective and meaningful test cases. In automation testing, testers perform the exact same steps used in manual testing, but with the assistance of a tool. Let's create the test scenario for our test case. **Test Scenario** A sequence of steps or actions designed to test a specific feature or functionality of an application is referred to as Test Scenario. - Launch the Chrome browser - Navigate to https://www.flipkart.com/ - Get the title of the web page - Close the Browser To execute the above test scenario, we create a test class in `src-->test-->java` directory. The test class serves as a container for organizing and executing the test cases related to a specific scenario or functionality ### 5.1 Creating a Test Class Let’s create a new Java file in our Java package and write our tests within it. We use "Test" as a suffix to the test classes as a Best Practice. In our test case, we will verify the title of the Flipkart web page. To represent this test case, we name our test class "FlipkartTitleTest". #### File: `FlipkartTitleTest.java` ```java public class FlipkartTitleTest{ } ``` Now let's execute the above test scenario. ### 5.2 Get Browser Title To get the browser title using Selenium, we should follow the below steps: 1. Set up ChromeDriver 2. Create a WebDriver instance 3. Navigate to the web page 4. Retrieve the page title 5. Quit the Browser Let's write our code to get the web page title. #### 5.3.1 Set up ChromeDriver To set up the Chrome driver, we will be writing the necessary code to configure and use it for our test automation. ```java public class FlipkartTitleTest { public static void main(String[] args) { System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); } } ``` Here, The `System.setProperty()` is used to tell the program where to find the ChromeDriver executable file on the system which interacts with the Chrome browser. We extract the downloaded ChromeDriver, copy the path of the executable chromedriver(.exe) and add it here. For Example: ```java System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "C:\\Users\\NewUser\\Downloads\\chromedriver_win32\\chromedriver.exe"); ``` #### Possible Issue Sometimes, extra quotes and forward slashes will be added after adding the ChromeDriver path. Remove them to avoid unexpected behaviour #### 5.3.2 Creating a WebDriver Instance To create a `WebDriver` instance and set up the Chrome driver, we can start by importing the necessary dependencies and writing the code. ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; public class FlipkartTitleTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); // Open the Chrome Browser WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); } } ``` Here, - We are creating an instance of `ChromeDriver` class which initializes the Chrome browser session and allows us to interact with the Chrome browser. - The `WebDriver` is a Java interface that provides a way to control a web browser and perform various actions on web elements. - The `WebDriver` serves as a bridge between the test script and the browser, allowing us to interact with web pages, navigate through them, and perform operations like verifying elements on the page. - The instance of `ChromeDriver` class initializes the Chrome browser session and allows us to interact with the chrome browser. The `ChromeDriver` class implements the `WebDriver` interface and provides the necessary methods to interact with the Chrome browser. Some of the methods of the WebDriver interface include: - `get(URL)`: Navigate the browser to the specified URL. It loads the web page associated with the given URL. - `getTitle()`: Retrieves the title of the current web page. It returns a string representing the title text. - `getCurrentUrl()`: Retrieves the URL of the current web page. It returns a string representing the current page's URL. - `click()`: Performs a click action on a web element, such as a button or a link. It simulates a user clicking on the element to trigger a specific action or navigation. #### 5.3.3 Navigate to the Web page To navigate to a web page using Selenium `WebDriver`, we use the methods provided by the `WebDriver` interface. The `get()` method of the `WebDriver` instance allows us to navigate to the specified URL ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; public class FlipkartTitleTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); // Navigate to the Flipkart page driver.get("http://www.flipkart.com"); } } ``` Here, the `get()` method is used to navigate our browser to the website "www.flipkart.com" and load its homepage. #### 5.3.4 Get Browser Title To get the title of the browser page using Selenium `WebDriver`, we can use the `getTitle()` method of the `Webdriver` interface. ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; public class FlipkartTitleTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); driver.get("http://www.flipkart.com"); //Get the web page title String title = driver.getTitle(); System.out.println(title); } } ``` Here, the `getTitle()` method of the `WebDriver` instance allows us to retrieve the title of the web page. #### 5.3.5 Quit the Browser Once we have obtained the title of the web page, it is crucial to close the browser properly to free up system resources. The `quit()` method is used to close the browser. The `quit()` method will close all the browser windows and tabs associated with the WebDriver instance. ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; public class FlipkartTitleTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); driver.get("http://www.flipkart.com"); String title = driver.getTitle(); System.out.println(title); driver.quit(); } } ``` Here, the `quit()` method is used to close the browser window and terminate the WebDriver session. We can also use `close()` method that closes the current browser window that the `WebDriver` instance is controlling. - If there is only one tab open, `close()` will close the entire window - If there are multiple tabs open, `close()`will close the active tab/currently working tab and the focus will shift to the next tab. We have completed building the code. Let's execute it. #### Executing the Tests Now that we have finished writing the code, it's time to execute it and see the output. - To run the code right click and select Run "FlipkartTitleTest.main()" as shown in the above picture. #### Output Here, we got the title of the web page of Flipkart. We can also notice a warning stating _"Unable to find CDP (Chrome DevTools Protocol) implementation"_. Please note that we can safely ignore this warning as it does not impact the automation process or the interactions with the web page.
### Summary - **Automation Testing:** Automation testing refers to the process of using software tools to automate the execution of tests, reducing manual effort and improving efficiency. - **Selenium Tool:** Selenium is a widely used open-source automation testing tool for web applications. - **Components of Selenium:** - Selenium consists of several components that work together: - **Selenium IDE:** Selenium IDE is a record-and-playback tool for creating and executing browser automation scripts. - **Selenium Grid:** Selenium Grid allows for parallel execution of tests on multiple machines and browsers simultaneously, improving test execution speed and efficiency. - **WebDriver:** WebDriver is a programming interface that provides a way to interact with web elements, simulate user actions, and manipulate the browser programmatically. - Setting up the Selenium Project: - Maven is a popular build and dependency management tool used to set up and manage Selenium projects. - Maven simplifies project configuration and allows for easy integration of Selenium dependencies. - Writing our first Selenium Test: - Java is a widely used programming language for writing Selenium tests. - Selenium WebDriver provides a Java API that allows us to interact with web elements, perform actions, and assert expected results. - Writing Selenium tests in Java involves setting up the development environment, creating test classes, utilizing WebDriver methods, and running the tests.
