# Automation Testing Using Selenium Part - 2
## Concepts Testing Login Functionality Writing automation Test Cases for the Login functionality Basic Terminologies WebElement Document Object Model Locators Web Element Actions
## Introduction In the previous session, we had discussed the fundamentals of automation testing and introduced Selenium, which is a widely used tool for automating the testing of web applications. We discussed the components of Selenium, set up a Selenium project using Maven, and learned writing first Selenium test using Java. #### NxtTrendz Web Application: In many web applications, there will be different pages that serve specific purposes. Assume, we have developed the application and now we need to test the application. It has different pages each has its own functionality and plays a role in providing a seamless user experience. Some of the pages of NxtTrendz Web Application include: - login page - home page - products page - product details page - cart page. In this unit, we will learn how to test a Login functionality of the NxtTrendz Web Application.
## 1. Testing Login Functionality So far, we have learned how to navigate to a web page and extract details such as the page title. Now, we have to test a simple login functionality. To test a login functionality, we can perform both manual testing and automation testing. ### 1.1 Testing Login Page Manually For successful login, we may follow the below steps: - Opening the Chrome Browser - Entering the URL of the application in browser - Entering username and password - Clicking on the login button So when we test a login functionality manually, it takes a lot of time because we have to keep going to the page, clear the fields, and enter different usernames and passwords to see if they work. It becomes repetitive and time consuming. Instead of us manually executing each step, automation testing allows us to break down them into systematic steps (test scenario) that can be performed automatically. Now we will use automation testing to verify the functionality of the login page effectively and efficiently. ### 1.2 Testing Login Page Automatically In manual testing, all tasks are performed manually, whereas in automation testing, scripts are written to automate the testing process. To test any feature of the application, we should first breakdown the manual steps into a systematic steps (Test Scenario). **Test Scenario** A test scenario can be defined as a sequence of steps or actions designed to test a specific feature or functionality of an application. Let's execute the above test scenario. ## 2. Writing automation Test Cases for the Login functionality We start the process of writing automation test cases by creating a project in the IntelliJ IDE. ### 2.1 Create Project Let's create a new project and name it as `LoginTest` for testing the login page. - Click on the create new project. - We choose JDK version 11. - Set group id and articat id. - Let's name the project as `LoginTest` and set our custom project location. - We have successfully created the project. Let's create the test class to write the test cases. ### 2.2 Create Test Class The test class serves as a container for organizing and executing the test cases related to a specific scenario or functionality.Now, we create a test class in `src-->test-->java` directory. In our test case, we test a login page. To represent this test case, we name our test class as "LoginTest". #### File: `LoginTest.java` ```java public class LoginTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ } } ``` ### 2.3 Integrating WebDriver To integrate WebDriver into our project, we need to add a specific dependency in the **pom.xml** file. After adding new dependencies to a Maven project, we need to reload the project to reflect the changes. We click on the above highlighted **Reload** button to reload the Maven project. We added required dependencies for our project. Let's begin by writing our test case to validate the functionality of the login page. ### 2.4 Setup Chrome Driver To set up the Chrome driver, we will be writing the necessary code to configure and use it for our test automation. ```java public class LoginTest { public static void main(String[] args) { // Set the path to the ChromeDriver executable System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); } } ``` Here, we provide the path of the Chrome driver as a string parameter to the `setProperty()` method. The `System.setProperty()` is used to tell the program where to find the chrome driver executable file on the system which interacts with the chrome browser. We extract the downloaded chrome driver, copy the path of the executable chromedriver(.exe) and add here. ### 2.5 Creating a WebDriver instance To create a `WebDriver` instance and set up the Chrome driver, we can start by importing the necessary dependencies and write the code. ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; public class LoginTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ // Set the path to the ChromeDriver executable System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); // Launch the Chrome Browser WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); } } ``` The `ChromeDriver` class implements the `WebDriver` interface and provides the necessary methods to interact with the Chrome browser Let's execute the code and check the output. #### Output ### 2.6 Navigate to the login page The `driver.get(URL)` method is used to naviate to the login page. ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; public class LoginTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ // Set the path to the ChromeDriver executable System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); // Launch the Chrome Browser WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); // Navigate to the login page driver.get("https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/login"); } } ``` Here, we are testing the login page of the website `https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/login`. Now, we need to automatically enter the values in username and password fields. ### 2.7 Enter username and password ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement; import org.openqa.selenium.By; public class LoginTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ // Set the path to the ChromeDriver executable System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); // Launch the Chrome Browser WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); // Navigate to the login page driver.get("https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/login"); // Find the username input element WebElement usernameEl = driver.findElement(By.id("username")); // Enter the username usernameEl.sendKeys("rahul"); } } ``` Let's execute the code and check the output. #### Output - Username rahul is automatically entered ## 3. Basic Terminologies In order to automate the process of entering values in the username and password fields, we first need to understand some basic concepts like: - WebElements - DOM - Locators ### 3.1 WebElement A web element is an HTML element that can be found on the web page. For example: Heading, Text fields, Buttons, Dropdowns etc. When a web page is loaded in a browser, the browser creates a structured representation of the page called the Document Object Model, or DOM ### 3.2 Document Object Model DOM is the structured representation of the content in the document created by the browser. It is a tree structured representation of HTML document created by the browser. #### HTML DOM Let's consider a simple HTML code snippet. This HTML code represents a basic webpage structure with a heading and a button element. #### HTML DOM Tree DOM tree for the above html code. #### Example Let's see the HTML DOM for the Nxt Trendz website (https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/login). #### Inspecting the web page We can also use the browser developer tools to see the HTML DOM. To find the HTML DOM of a web page, we need to inspect the web page using browser developer tools. We follow the below steps to inspect the web page. - Select "Inspect" from the menu that appears - Select the Elements tab to see the HTML code - Explore the HTML code by expanding and collapsing elements In order to interact with different web elements on a web page, such as text fields, buttons, checkboxes, and links, it is necessary to first locate them. We can use locators to locate various elements on a webpage during automation testing. Let's learn about locators. ### 3.3 Locators Locators are used to identify an HTML element on a web page. Locators are one of the essential components of Selenium infrastructure, which help Selenium scripts in uniquely identifying the WebElements(such as text box, button, etc.) present on the web page. There are various types of locators, using which we can identify a web element uniquely on the web page | Locator | Usage | | :---------------: | :------------------------------------------------ | | Id | Locates an element using the ID attribute | | Class Name | Locates an element using the Class attribute | | CSS Selector | Locates an element using the CSS selector | | Link Text | Locates a link using link text | | XPath | Locates an element using an XPath expression | | Name | Locates an element using the Name attribute | | Tag Name | Locates elements based on their HTML tag | | Partial Link Text | Locates a link using a partial match on link text | When using Selenium to locate web elements, it is generally preferred to prioritize the use of the id attribute. Let’s locate the username and password elements using id attribute ### 3.4 Using id attribute Now we locate the username field based on its `id` attribute. **3.4.1 Locating Username Element** To locate an element on the web page, follow below steps: - Right click on the element - Select the inspect - Find the element Here, id of the username web element is **username**. **3.4.2 Find Username Web Element** We find the web element using the `findElement()` method provided by the `WebDriver`. #### Syntax ```java WebElement element = driver.findElement(By.locatorStrategy("locator")); WebElement usernameEl = driver.findElement(By.id("username")); ``` Here, - `WebElement` is an interface provided by Selenium that represents web element on a web page. - `element` is the variable name chosen to store the reference to the single web element. - `driver` is an instance of the Selenium WebDriver that represents the web browser. - `findElement()` is a method provided by the driver object to locate a single web element on the web page. - `By` is a class provided by Selenium that offers various locator strategies to find web elements. - `locatorStrategy` represents the specific locator strategy we want to use, such as `id`, `name`, `className`, `xpath`, `cssSelector`, and others. - `locator` is the value we provide to the locator strategy. It can be an ID, class name, name, XPath expression, CSS selector, or any other value that helps identify the element we want to find. In manual testing, we manually enter the username and password and click the button to perform the action. In automation testing, we use code to interact with web elements and perform these actions automatically. Let's learn about the different web element actions. ## 4. Web Element Actions Selenium provides a set of methods to interact with web elements automatically. These methods can be used to perform actions such as clicking on elements, entering text, and submitting forms. Here are some of the most commonly used Selenium methods for interacting with web elements: - click() - sendKeys() - clear() - submit() | Methods | Usage | | :--------: | :----------------------------------------------------------------- | | click() | This method clicks on the specified web element. | | sendKeys() | This method enters text into the specified web element. | | clear() | This method clears the text from the specified web element | | submit() | This method submits the form containing the specified web element. | To automate the process of entering text into web elements, we can utilize the `sendKeys()` method provided by Selenium. This method allows us to programmatically input text into input fields, text areas. ### 4.1 Enter the Username We use the `sendKeys()` method to enter the username. In our case the username is `rahul` #### Syntax ```java element.sendKeys(Charsequence); element.sendKeys("rahul"); ``` `sendKeys()` method in Selenium allows us to type text into a web element. It takes the text as input and sets it as the value of the element. Let's find the password web element based on its id attribute. ### 4.2 Locating the Password Element Now locate the password web element using id attribute Here, the id of the password web element is `password`. Now we locate the password web element using id attribute. Let's write the code to find the password web element. ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement; import org.openqa.selenium.By; public class LoginTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ // Set the path to the ChromeDriver executable System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); // Launch the Chrome Browser WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); // Navigate to the login page driver.get("https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/login"); // Find the username input element WebElement usernameEl = driver.findElement(By.id("username")); // Enter the username usernameEl.sendKeys("rahul"); // Find the password input element WebElement passwordEl = driver.findElement(By.id("password")); // Enter the password passwordEl.sendKeys("rahul@2021"); } } ``` Here, we are using the `findElement()` method to locate the password web element on a web page. The method returns an object of type `WebElement`, which is assigned to the variable `passwordEl`. Let's execute the code and check the output. #### Output - Password `rahul@2021` is automatically entered. Similarly, let's locate the login button . ### 4.3 Locating the Login Button Here, we don’t have the `id` attribute for button element, but using the `class` attribute we can locate it. The value of the class attribute for login button is `login-button`. We locate the login button based on its `class` attribute. If we use `findElement()` on elements with the same class name, it will locate and return the first matching element it finds. Let's write the code to find the login button web element. ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement; import org.openqa.selenium.By; public class LoginTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ // Set the path to the ChromeDriver executable System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); // Launch the Chrome Browser WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); // Navigate to the login page driver.get("https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/login"); // Find the username input element WebElement usernameEl = driver.findElement(By.id("username")); // Enter the username usernameEl.sendKeys("rahul"); // Find the password input element WebElement passwordEl = driver.findElement(By.id("password")); // Enter the password passwordEl.sendKeys("rahul@2021"); // Find the submit button element WebElement submitButtonElement = driver.findElement(By.className("login-button")); // Click the submit button submitButtonElement.submit(); } } ``` To automate the submission of forms or triggering actions on web pages, we can use the `submit()` method provided by Selenium. Let's execute the code and check the output. #### Output We have successfully entered the username and password and submit the login button. As a result, we expect the user to be redirected to the home page. To verify successful navigation to the home page after the login action, we can follow these simple steps: - Define the expected URL of the home page. - Get the current URL using `getCurrentUrl()` in Selenium. - Compare the current URL with the expected URL. - If the URLs match, the navigation to the home page was successful. - If they don't match, there might be a navigation issue. Let's verify whether the navigation was successful or not by following the above steps. ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement; import org.openqa.selenium.By; public class LoginTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ // Set the path to the ChromeDriver executable System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); // Launch the Chrome Browser WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); // Navigate to the login page driver.get("https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/login"); // Find the username input element WebElement usernameEl = driver.findElement(By.id("username")); // Enter the username usernameEl.sendKeys("rahul"); // Find the password input element WebElement passwordEl = driver.findElement(By.id("password")); // Enter the password passwordEl.sendKeys("rahul@2021"); // Find the submit button element WebElement submitButtonElement = driver.findElement(By.className("login-button")); // Click the submit button submitButtonElement.submit(); // Define the expected URL of the home page String expectedUrl = "https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/"; // Get the current URL after login String currentUrl = driver.getCurrentUrl(); if(currentUrl.equals(expectedUrl)){ System.out.println("Navigation to home page was successful!"); }else{ System.out.println("Navigation to home page failed!"); } } } ``` Here, we are utilizing the getCurrentUrl() method to retrieve the current URL of the web page we are currently on. If we are logged in successfully if will print "Navigation to home page was successful!". Otherwise it will print "Navigation to home page failed!". Let's execute the code and verify a successful login. #### Output Here, the output is "Navigation to home page failed!". Even though we entered the correct username and password, it shows the login process was unsuccessful. Let's know the reason behind it. #### Delay in Webpage Loading When we navigate to a new page on a website, sometimes there can be a small delay in the webpage getting fully loaded. During this delay, the browser is working to load and display all the content on the webpage While the browser is doing this, our code tries to get the current URL using `driver.getCurrentUrl()` to compare it with the expected URL. To handle such situations, we can introduce a delay or pause in our code. It allows the necessary elements on the webpage to be fully loaded before we perform any actions or check. ### WebDriverWait In Selenium, we have a useful class called `WebDriverWait`. It helps us wait for specific conditions to be met before proceeding with the execution of our code. By using the `WebDriverWait` class, we can specify a timeout duration and the expected condition that needs to be fulfilled The class will wait for the condition to be true within the specified timeout period. **Syntax** ```java WebDriverWait wait = new WebDriverWait(driver, Duration.ofSeconds(10)); wait.until(ExpectedConditions.urlToBe(expectedUrl)); ``` Here, - `WebDriverWait`: It is a class provided by Selenium WebDriver that allows us to wait for a certain condition to be met before proceeding with the execution of the code. - `wait`: It is an instance of the WebDriverWait class that we are creating. - `Duration.ofSeconds(10)`: It tells the object to wait for a maximum of 10 seconds for the condition to be met. - `driver`: It refers to the `WebDriver` instance that is controlling the browser. - `wait.until()`: It is a method provided by WebDriverWait that waits until a specific condition is met. - `ExpectedConditions.urlToBe(expectedUrl)`: It is a condition provided by `ExpectedConditions` class that checks if the current URL matches the expected URL. The `until` method of the wait object waits until the condition is true or until the maximum waiting time (10 seconds in our case) is reached. Let's add the delay before performing the `getCurrentUrl()` method. ### Adding Delay ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement; import org.openqa.selenium.By; import org.openqa.selenium.support.ui.ExpectedConditions; import org.openqa.selenium.support.ui.WebDriverWait; import java.time.Duration; public class LoginTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ // Set the path to the ChromeDriver executable System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); // Launch the Chrome Browser WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); // Navigate to the login page driver.get("https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/login"); // Find the username input element WebElement usernameEl = driver.findElement(By.id("username")); // Enter the username usernameEl.sendKeys("rahul"); // Find the password input element WebElement passwordEl = driver.findElement(By.id("password")); // Enter the password passwordEl.sendKeys("rahul@2021"); // Find the submit button element WebElement submitButtonElement = driver.findElement(By.className("login-button")); // Click the submit button submitButtonElement.submit(); // Define the expected URL of the home page String expectedUrl = "https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/"; // Wait for the expected URL to be loaded WebDriverWait wait = new WebDriverWait(driver, Duration.ofSeconds(10)); wait.until(ExpectedConditions.urlToBe(expectedUrl)); // Get the current URL after login String currentUrl = driver.getCurrentUrl(); if(currentUrl.equals(expectedUrl)){ System.out.println("Navigation to home page was successful!"); }else{ System.out.println("Navigation to home page failed!"); } } } ``` Here, we have added a delay before retrieving the URL of the page following a successful login. Let's run the code and verify a successful login. #### Output Hurray!, we have successfully verified the login functionality of the web page. Lets write the code to quit the browser. The `quit()` method is used to close the Chrome browser ```java import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement; import org.openqa.selenium.By; import org.openqa.selenium.support.ui.ExpectedConditions; import org.openqa.selenium.support.ui.WebDriverWait; import java.time.Duration; public class LoginTest{ public static void main(String[] args){ // Set the path to the ChromeDriver executable System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); // Launch the Chrome Browser WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); // Navigate to the login page driver.get("https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/login"); // Find the username input element WebElement usernameEl = driver.findElement(By.id("username")); // Enter the username usernameEl.sendKeys("rahul"); // Find the password input element WebElement passwordEl = driver.findElement(By.id("password")); // Enter the password passwordEl.sendKeys("rahul@2021"); // Find the submit button element WebElement submitButtonElement = driver.findElement(By.className("login-button")); // Click the submit button submitButtonElement.submit(); // Define the expected URL of the home page String expectedUrl = "https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/"; // Wait for the expected URL to be loaded WebDriverWait wait = new WebDriverWait(driver, Duration.ofSeconds(10)); wait.until(ExpectedConditions.urlToBe(expectedUrl)); // Get the current URL after login String currentUrl = driver.getCurrentUrl(); if(currentUrl.equals(expectedUrl)){ System.out.println("Navigation to home page was successful!"); }else{ System.out.println("Navigation to home page failed!"); } // Quit the WebDriver instance driver.quit(); } } ``` ```
### Summary - Automation testing allows us to break down them into systematic steps (test scenario) that can be performed automatically. - In order to automate the process of entering values in the input fields, we first need to understand some basic concepts: - WebElement: A webelement is an HTML element that can be found on the web page - DOM: DOM is the structured representation of the content in the document created by the browser - Locators: Locators are the way to identify an HTML element on a web page. - There are various types of locators, using which we can identify a web element uniquely on the Webpage - ID: Locates an element using the ID attribute. - ClassName: Locates an element using the Class attribute. - CSS Selector: Locates an element using the CSS selector. - Link Text: Locates a link using link text. - XPath: Locates an element using an XPath expression - Name: Locates an element using the Name attribute - The `findElement()` is a method provided by the driver object to locate a single web element on the web page. - Selenium provides a set of methods to perform some actions such as clicking on elements, entering text, and submitting forms. - `click()`: This method clicks on the specified web element. - `sendKeys()`: This method enters text into the specified web element. - `clear()`: This method clears the text from the specified web element - `submit()`: This method submits the form containing the specified web element.

## Coding Practice - 2

### Login Test 1 In this exercise, you will be automating entering username in a login form. ### Prerequisites - Install IntelliJ IDEA Community IDE Version 2018.3.6. - Install OpenJDK 11 and complete the configuration. - Install a Browser Driver(Chrome Driver). - Setup a Selenium project with the name `LoginTest1`. You can refer to this [Reading Material](https://learning.ccbp.in/qa-automation-testing/course?c_id=cf952b35-27ab-4b1e-a6de-44227f22806c&s_id=f5c19277-3889-4e63-b631-c06c088d612c&t_id=6a935df7-2c93-477c-b505-3ae0aabcf9a2#31-installing-ide) to complete the above prerequisites. ### Steps to Automate - Create a driver instance using WebDriver interface. - Navigate to the url `https://qaebank.ccbp.tech/ebank/login` - Enter the username and print "Username entered" - _use id locator_. - Close the browser window. >

You can refer to this [Reading Material](https://learning.ccbp.in/qa-automation-testing/course?c_id=cf952b35-27ab-4b1e-a6de-44227f22806c&s_id=f5c19277-3889-4e63-b631-c06c088d612c&t_id=6a935df7-2c93-477c-b505-3ae0aabcf9a2#31-installing-ide) to complete the above prerequisites. ### Steps to Automate - Create a driver instance using WebDriver interface. - Navigate to the url `https://qaebank.ccbp.tech/ebank/login` - Enter the username and print "Username entered" - _use id locator_. - Enter the password and print "Password entered"- _use id locator_. - Submit the login form and print "Submitted login details" - _use className locator_. - Close the browser window. >

>Try to solve it on your own before checking the solution. > >- Click [here](https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/LoginTest2.zip) for the solution. >- Extract the downloaded file and open it in your local IDE (IntelliJ) to check the solution. >
### Login Test 3 In this exercise, you will be automating entering username and password, clicking "Submit" button in a login form and verify the login status. ### Prerequisites - Install IntelliJ IDEA Community IDE Version 2018.3.6. - Install OpenJDK 11 and complete the configuration. - Install a Browser Driver(Chrome Driver). - Setup a Selenium project with the name `LoginTest3`. You can refer to this [Reading Material](https://learning.ccbp.in/qa-automation-testing/course?c_id=cf952b35-27ab-4b1e-a6de-44227f22806c&s_id=f5c19277-3889-4e63-b631-c06c088d612c&t_id=6a935df7-2c93-477c-b505-3ae0aabcf9a2#31-installing-ide) to complete the above prerequisites. ### Steps to Automate - Create a driver instance using WebDriver interface. - Navigate to the url `https://qaebank.ccbp.tech/ebank/login` - Enter the username and print "Username entered" - _use id locator_. - Enter the password and print "Password entered"- _use id locator_. - Submit the login form and print "Submitted login details" - _use className locator_. - Wait for a maximum of 10 seconds for the web page to be redirected. - Verify if the current URL matches the expected URL (https://qaebank.ccbp.tech/). - If both expected and current URLs are same - Print "Logged in successfully" - Print current page title in a new line. - Close the browser window. >
>Need help? >
>Try to solve it on your own before checking the solution. > >- Click [here](https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/LoginTest3.zip) for the solution. >- Extract the downloaded file and open it in your local IDE (IntelliJ) to check the solution. >
### Login Test 4 In this exercise, you will be automating entering username and password, clicking "Submit" button in a login form, verify the login status and logging out from the web site. ### Prerequisites - Install IntelliJ IDEA Community IDE Version 2018.3.6. - Install OpenJDK 11 and complete the configuration. - Install a Browser Driver(Chrome Driver). - Setup a Selenium project with the name `LoginTest4`. # XPath Axes
## Concepts XPath Axes Parent Axis Child Axis Following-Sibling Axis Preceding-Sibling Axis Descendant Axis Ancestor Axis Testing Product Rating
## Introduction In the previous unit, we focused on testing the functionality of the products page and the product details page. We verified that products were displayed correctly on the products page and that product details were accurately presented on the product details page. In this unit, we will be testing the rating of the product on the products page of the NxtTrendz application. Click [here](https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/ProductsPageTest.zip) to download the initial code for this project.
## 1. XPath So far, we have successfully tested the below functionalities: - Logging into the application - Navigating to the home page - Navigating to the products page and verifying the display of products Now, we are going to test the rating of the product on the products page of the NxtTrendz application. Before we can test the rating of a product, we need to locate the element that contains the rating information In the DOM, there are multiple elements with the same tag name, class name, and display text. **How can we distinguish and accurately identify the particular element?** We learned that XPath in Selenium offers various approaches for finding elements. A few commonly used approaches for locating elements using XPath: 1. Absolute XPath 2. Relative XPath 3. XPath Functions 4. XPath Axes When we encounter multiple elements that have the same tag, class name, and text, XPath Axes can be used to accurately identify the specific element.
## 2. XPath Axes In Selenium, XPath axes are used to find elements in an HTML document based on their relationship to the current node. XPath axes provide a way to traverse the document structure relative to a particular context node. Some of the most commonly used XPath axes in Selenium: - Parent - Child - Following and Preceding Sibling - Descendant - Ancestor Let's learn about each XPath axis and use them to locate elements in our project. ### 2.1 Parent Axis To use XPath axes, we need to have a starting point in the HTML document. This starting point is called the current node or context node. The parent element of the current node refers to the immediate element that directly contains or wraps the current node in the DOM hierarchy. Let's understand this with the example **Example** Let's consider the sample "Book Store" HTML DOM. The tree representation of the "Book Store" DOM is as follows. We have a separate `
` tag for each book in the "Book Store" HTML DOM. Let's consider the `
` tag related to the "Harry Potter" book as the current node. Let's see the above `
` element in the DOM tree. We consider the second `
` element that is related to "Harry Potter" as the current node. We know that the parent element of the current node refers to the immediate element that directly contains or wraps the current node. So the parent node will be the `
` with the class name `bookstore`. Let's see the above mentioned parent node in the DOM tree. Now we understood the parent and child relationship in the HTML DOM. Let's use the XPath axes to write the XPath expressions. To find any element using XPath axes, we need to follow these steps: - Identify the current node in the DOM hierarchy - Use the XPath axes to select the elements of the current node Let's locate the parent element(`
` with class name `bookstore`) of the current node (`
` with category value `children`). The XPath expression would be, `//div[@category='children']/parent::div`. Here, - `//div`: Selects all `
` elements anywhere in the DOM hierarchy. - `[@category='children']`: Filters the selected `
` elements based on the condition that their `category` attribute value is 'children'. - `/parent::div`: Selects the parent element of the filtered `
` element, which must be a `
` element. To select a specific element using XPath expressions in the DOM hierarchy within a browser we follow the below steps: 1. Inspect the web page 2. Press Ctrl + F (or Cmd + F) to open the search bar 3. Enter the XPath expression 4. The matching elements will be highlighted Let's select the `
` element with `category` value `children` using the XPath expression, `//div[@category='children']/parent::div`. Let's learn another XPath axis called `child` and understand how it can be used in XPath expressions. ### 2.2 Child Axis The XPath axis `child` is used to identify and select the child elements of the current node. The Child elements are the immediate elements that are nested within and directly under the current node in the DOM hierarchy. Let's see the child elements of our current node(`
` with `category` as `children`) in the DOM tree of "Book Store". The XPath expression would be, `//div[@category='children']/child::*` Here, - `//div`: Selects all `
` elements anywhere in the DOM hierarchy. - `[@category='children']`: Filters the selected `
` elements based on the condition that their `category` attribute value is 'children'. - `/child::`: Used to select the child elements of the current node. - `*`: The `*` is a symbol that matches all the elements under the specified node. Here, it matches all the child elements. #### Asterik(*) The asterisk (*) in XPath is used to match and select any element within the given context. It doesn't specify a particular element type or name, allowing you to select elements of any type as children, regardless of their tag name. If we use "h1" instead of the asterisk (*) in an XPath expression, it will specifically select all child elements of the specified type. In this case, the "h1" elements. Let's select the child elements of the current node(`
` with `category` as `children`) in the HTML DOM hierarchy. Here, we can observe that the search result matches 2 elements, and we can navigate between them using the up and down arrows, with each matched element being highlighted when selected. Let's learn another XPath axis called `following-sibling` and understand how it can be used in XPath expressions. ### 2.3 Following-Sibling Axis The XPath axis `following-sibling` is used to identify and select the sibling elements that come after the current node. Siblings are at the same level as the current node and share its parent. It specifically selects the sibling elements that appear after the current node, excluding the current node itself or any siblings that come before it. Let us write the XPath expression to select the following siblings of the current node, which is the `
` element with the `category` attribute value of `children`. The XPath expression would be, `//div[@category='children']/following-sibling::*`. Here, - `//div`: Selects all `
` elements. - `[@category='children']`: Filters the selected `
` elements based on the condition that they have a category attribute with the value 'children'. - `/following-sibling::*`: Selects all sibling elements that appear after the filtered `
` elements. Let's select the following sibling elements of our current node(`
` with `category` as `children`) in the DOM tree of "Book Store". Let's learn another XPath axis called `preceding-sibling` and understand how it can be used in XPath expressions. ### 2.4 Preceding-Sibling Axis The XPath axis `preceding-sibling` is used to identify and select the sibling elements that come before the current node. It specifically selects the sibling elements that appear before the current node, excluding the current node itself or any siblings that come after it. Let us write the XPath expression to select the preceding siblings of the current node, which is the `
` element with the `category` attribute value of `children`. The Xpath expression would be, `//div[@category='children']/preceding-sibling::*` Here, - `//div`: Selects all `
` elements. - `[@category='children']`: Filters the selected `
` elements based on the condition that they have a category attribute with the value 'children'. - `/preceding-sibling::*`: Selects all sibling elements that appear before the filtered `
` elements. Let's select the preceding sibling elements of our current node(`
` with `category` as `children`) in the DOM tree of "Book Store". Let's learn another XPath axis called `descendant` and understand how it can be used in XPath expressions. ### 2.5 Descendant Axis The XPath axis `descendant` is used to identify and select all descendant elements of the context node or current node. Descendant elements include all elements that are nested within the current node at any level in the DOM hierarchy, not just the immediate children. Let us write the XPath expression to select all the descendant elements of the current node, which is the `
` element with the `category` attribute value of `children`. The XPath expression would be, `//div[@category='children']/descendant::*`. Here, - `//div`: Selects all `
` elements in the document. - `[@category='children']`: Filters the selected `
` elements to only those that have the attribute category with a value of 'children'. - `/descendant::*`: Selects all descendant elements of the filtered `
` elements. Let's select the descendant elements of our current node(`
` with `category` as `children`) in the DOM tree of "Book Store". In the above image, we can see that there are five descendants for the current node, which is the `
` element with the `category` attribute value of `children`. Let's learn another XPath axis called `ancestor` and understand how it can be used in XPath expressions. ### 2.6 Ancestor Axis The XPath axis `ancestor` is used to identify and select all ancestor elements of the current node. Ancestor elements include all elements that are the parent, grandparent, great-grandparent, etc. of the current node, all the way up to the root node(``). Here, `

`, ``, `<head>`, etc elements are not the ancestors of the current node. Let us write the XPath expression to select all the ancestor elements of the current node, which is the `<div>` element with the `category` attribute value of `children`. The XPath expression would be, `//div[@category='children']/ancestor::*`. Here, - `//div`: Selects all `<div>` elements in the document. - `[@category='children']`: Filters the selected `<div>` elements to only those that have the attribute category with a value of 'children'. - `/ancestor::*`: Selects all ancestor elements(upto root node) of the filtered `<div>` elements. Let's see all the ancestor elements of our current node(`<div>` with `category` as `children`) in the DOM tree of "Book Store". <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-ancestor-search.png" alt="ancestor elements"> In the above image, we can see that there are three ancestor elements for the current node, which is the `<div>` element with the `category` attribute value of `children`. Let's learn how XPath axes can be used in an E-commerce application to locate elements more effectively. </Section> <Section> ## 3. Testing Product Rating To test product rating functionality, we should first create the project and then we should write the tests, - Login functionality - Navigating to the home page - Navigating to the products page - Verifying the display of products, etc. To avoid repeating the above steps every time, we can utilize the initial code provided in the [Introduction](#introduction) section. Extract the Downloaded Zip and open the project using IntelliJ. ### 3.1 Initial Code - Test Steps The initial code provides all the respective code to automate the below steps, 1. Launch Chrome Browser 2. Navigate to the login page 3. Enter the username and password 4. Click on the login button 5. User should be able to redirect to the home page 6. On the home page, locate and click on the "Shop Now" button 7. User should be able to redirect to the Products Page 8. Validate the display of products Execute the initial code in the `ProductsRatingTest.java` file. #### Output ``` Navigation to home page was successful! Navigation to products page was successful! Products are displayed successfully on the products page: 57 ``` Let's locate the product rating using XPath Axes. <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-product-rating.png" alt="product rating"> In order to find the rating of a product using XPath, we must first identify the current node ### 3.2 Locating Current Node We can use the unique `h1` element with the text "Minifigures" as the current node. <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-h1-current-node.png" alt="current node"> Let's locate the current node using the `text()` function. The XPath expression would be, `//h1[text()='Minifigures']`. ```java // Select Product with text Minifigures WebElement productRatingEle = driver.findElement(By.xpath("//h1[text()='Minifigures']")); ``` Let's observe the HTML code of the products page to understand how we can use XPath axes for element selection. <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-html-code.png" alt="html dom tree"> The DOM tree of the above code would be, <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-html-dom-tree.png" alt="dom tree for above html"> Let's find the product rating element. ### 3.3 Finding Product Rating Element There are several ways to find the product rating element. Let's learn one of them <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-access-rating-ele.png" alt="access rating element dom tree"> - Selecting following-sibling `<div>` element - Access the product rating element. The XPath expression for selecting the following-sibling `<div>` element would be, `//h1[text()='Minifigures']/following-sibling::div`. Now, let's add the relative XPath at the end of the above XPath expression to locate the product rating element. The XPath expression to locate the product rating element would be, `//h1[text()='Minifigures']/following-sibling::div//p[@class='rating']` <MultiLineNote> We can use both absolute and relative XPath in the single Xpath expression. The `//` allows searching for elements anywhere in the DOM hierarchy and is commonly used in relative XPath expression, while `/` is used to select immediate child elements in absolute XPath or select elements based on specific axis such as `parent`, `child`, `following-sibling`, `preceding-sibling`, `ancestor`, `descendant`, etc., </MultiLineNote> Let us write the code to verify the product rating. ```java String expectedRating = "3.9"; WebElement productRatingEle = driver.findElement(By.xpath("//h1[text()='Minifigures']/following-sibling::div//p[@class='rating']")); String rating = productRatingEle.getText(); if(expectedRating.equals(rating)){ System.out.println("Rating is 3.9"); } ``` Let's add the above code to our existing code so that it verifies the product rating only after all the products have been fully loaded. ```java import org.openqa.selenium.By; import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; import java.time.Duration; import org.openqa.selenium.support.ui.ExpectedConditions; import org.openqa.selenium.support.ui.WebDriverWait; import java.util.List; public class ProductRatingTest { public static void main(String args[]){ System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER"); // Open the Chrome Browser WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); // Open the NxtTrendz login page driver.get("https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/login"); // Find and fill in the form fields WebElement usernameEl = driver.findElement(By.xpath("//input[@id='username']")); usernameEl.sendKeys("rahul"); WebElement passwordEl = driver.findElement(By.xpath("//input[@id='password']")); passwordEl.sendKeys("rahul@2021"); WebElement buttonEl = driver.findElement(By.xpath("//button[@type='submit']")); buttonEl.submit(); // Define the expected URL of the home page String homePageUrl= "https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/"; // Wait for the expected URL to be loaded WebDriverWait wait = new WebDriverWait(driver, Duration.ofSeconds(10)); wait.until(ExpectedConditions.urlToBe(homePageUrl)); // Get the current URL after login String currentUrl = driver.getCurrentUrl(); if(currentUrl.equals(homePageUrl)){ System.out.println("Navigation to home page was successful!"); }else{ System.out.println("Navigation to home page failed!"); } // Find and click on the "Shop Now" button WebElement shopNowButtonEl = driver.findElement(By.xpath("//button[@class='shop-now-button']")); shopNowButtonEl.click(); // Define the expected URL of the products page String productsPageUrl = "https://rahulnxttrendz.ccbp.tech/products"; // Get the current URL after navigating to the products page currentUrl = driver.getCurrentUrl(); if(currentUrl.equals(productsPageUrl)){ System.out.println("Navigation to products page was successful!"); } //Wait until elements are displayed wait.until(ExpectedConditions.visibilityOfElementLocated(By.xpath("//li[@class='product-item']"))); // Verify the display of products on the products page List<WebElement> products = driver.findElements(By.xpath("//li[@class='product-item']")); if (products.size() > 0) { System.out.println("Products are displayed successfully on the products page: "+ products.size()); String expectedRating = "3.9"; WebElement productRatingEle = driver.findElement(By.xpath("//h1[text()='Minifigures']/following-sibling::div//p[@class='rating']")); String rating = productRatingEle.getText(); if(expectedRating.equals(rating)){ System.out.println("Rating is 3.9"); } } else { System.out.println("No products found on the products page."); } // Close the browser driver.quit(); } } ``` Let's run the above code to check the output. #### Output ``` Navigation to home page was successful! Navigation to products page was successful! Products are displayed successfully on the products page: 57 Rating is 3.9 ``` Here, we can see that the product rating is as expected. Let's learn the remaining XPath axes and learn how to use them effectively. Let's learn another XPath axis called the `following` and understand how it can be used in XPath expressions. ### 3.4 Following Axis The XPath axis `following` is used to identify and select all elements that appear after the context node in the DOM hierarchy. The `following` axis includes all sibling elements and their descendants that come after the current node. It does not include the current node, its descendants, and its ancestors. Let's observe the DOM tree of the "Book Store" application and understand the `following` axis. <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-following1.png" alt="following tree"> Let us write the XPath expression to select all the following elements of the current node, which is the `<div>` element with the `category` attribute value of `children`. The XPath expression would be, `//div[@category="children"]/following::*`. Here, - `//div`: Selects all `<div>` elements in the document. - `[@category="children"]`: Filters the selected `<div>` elements based on the condition that their category attribute value is equal to "children". - `/following::*`: Selects all the sibling elements and their descendants that come after the filtered `<div>` elements in the document hierarchy. Let's select all the following elements of our current node(`<div>` with `category` as `children`) in the DOM tree of "Book Store". <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-html-following.png" alt="html following"> In the above image, we can observe that there are 13 elements in the DOM hierarchy that come after the `<div>` element with the `category` attribute value of `children`. Let's learn another XPath axis called `preceding` and understand how it can be used in XPath expressions. ### 3.5 Preceding Axis The XPath axis `preceding` is used to identify and select all elements that appear before the context node in the DOM hierarchy, excluding the ancestor elements of the elements that come after the context node. It does not include the current node and its descendants. Let's observe the DOM tree of the "Book Store" application and understand the `preceding` axis. <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-preceding1.png" alt="preceding elements tree"> Here, we can observe that `<html>`, `<body>`, and `<div>` are not selected because they are ancestor elements of the elements that appear after the context node. It will also select `<head>`, `<title>`, and so on, as they are not the ancestor elements of the elements that appear after the context node. Let us write the XPath expression to select all the preceding elements of the current node, which is the `<div>` element with the `category` attribute value of `children`. The XPath expression would be, `//div[@category="children"]/preceding::*`. Here, - `//div`: Selects all `<div>` elements in the document. - `[@category="children"]`: Filters the selected `<div>` elements based on the condition that their category attribute value is equal to "children". - `/preceding::*`: Selects all elements that appear before the filtered `<div>` elements in the DOM hierarchy. Let's select all the following elements of our current node(`<div>` with `category` as `children`) in the DOM tree of "Book Store". <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-html-preceding1.png" alt="preceding html"> Let's learn another XPath axis called `ancestor-or-self` and understand how it can be used in XPath expressions. ### 3.6 Ancestor-or-Self Axis The XPath axis `ancestor-or-self` is used to identify and select the context node and all its ancestor elements in the DOM hierarchy. The `ancestor-or-self` axis includes the current node itself and all its ancestors up to the root node. Let's observe the DOM tree of the "Book Store" application and understand the `ancestor-or-self` axis. <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-updatedpic.png" alt="ancestor or self"> Let us write the XPath expression to select all the ancestor elements of the current node, including the current node itself(`<div>` element with the `category` attribute value of `children`). The XPath expression would be, `//div[@category="children"]/ancestor-or-self::*`. Here, - `//div`: Selects all `<div>` elements in the document. - `[@category="children"]`: Filters the selected `<div>` elements based on the condition that their category attribute value is equal to "children". - `/ancestor-or-self::*`: Selects all the ancestor elements of the filtered `<div>` elements, including the `<div>` elements themselves. Let's select all the ancestors and the current node itself (`<div>` with `category` as `children`) in the DOM tree of "Book Store". <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-html-ancestor-or.png" alt="ancestor or self html"> Let's learn another XPath axis called `descendant-or-self` and understand how it can be used in XPath expressions. ### 3.7 Descendant-or-Self Axis The XPath axis `descendant-or-self` is used to identify and select the context node and all its descendant elements in the DOM hierarchy. The `descendant-or-self` axis includes the current node itself and all its descendants at any level in the DOM hierarchy. Let's observe the DOM tree of the "Book Store" application and understand the `descendant-or-self` axis. <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-descendant-or.png" alt="descendant or self"> Let us write the XPath expression to select all the descendant elements of the current node, including the current node itself(`<div>` element with the `category` attribute value of `children`). The XPath expression would be, `//div[@category="children"]/descendant-or-self::*`. Here, - `//div`: Selects all `<div>` elements in the document, regardless of their position. - `[@category='children']`: Filters the selected `<div>` elements based on the condition that their category attribute value is equal to 'children'. - `/descendant-or-self::*`: Selects all descendants or self of the filtered `<div>` elements, including the `<div>` elements themselves. The * represents any element node. Let's select all the descendant elements and the current node itself (`<div>` with `category` as `children`) in the DOM tree of "Book Store". <Img imageSrc="https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/images/qa-rm-10-html-descendant-or.png" alt="descendant or"> Here, we can observe that it selects all 6 descendants along with the current node where the current node is highlighted. **XPath Axes with position() function** We are aware of the `position()` function in XPath, which is used to determine the position of an element within a set of selected elements. While using the `position()` function with XPath axes, the function returns the position of the element concerning the current node, but not concerning the position in the HTML DOM. This means that for a few axes (like `child`, `following-sibling`, `descendant`, `following`, and `descendant-or-self`), the position is increasing from **top to bottom** of the HTML DOM while for others (like `preceding-sibling`, `ancestor`, `preceding`, and `ancestor-or-self`), the position is increasing from **bottom to top** of the HTML DOM. <Img imageSrc="https://res.cloudinary.com/dercsvrre/image/upload/v1694421661/QA%20MCQs/yqopps3b65iarumlwtfz.png" alt="qa-rm-xpath-axes-with-position"> For example, consider the current node as the `<div>` element with the class attribute value of `book` at position `2`. The ancestors of the current node are the `<div>` element with the class name `bookstore`, `<body>` element, and the `<html>` element. We use the below XPath expressions to select the desired elements, | Desired element | XPath expression | | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | | `<div>` element with the class name `bookstore` | `//div[@class='book'][2]/ancestor::*[position() = 1]` | | `<body>` element | `//div[@class='book'][2]/ancestor::*[position() = 2]` | | `<html>` element | `//div[@class='book'][2]/ancestor::*[position() = 3]` | From the above table, we can understand that the position while using the ancestor axis will be in the increasing order from bottom to top of the HTML DOM. Whereas, the position while using the descendant axis will be in the increasing order from top to bottom of the HTML DOM as shown below, | Desired element | XPath expression | | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | | `<h1>` element with class name `title` | `//div[@class='book'][2]/descendant::*[position() = 1]` | | `<div>` element with class name `book-details` | `//div[@class='book'][2]/descendant::*[position() = 2]` | | `<p>` element with class name `author` | `//div[@class='book'][2]/descendant::*[position() = 3]` | | `<div>` element with class name `year` | `//div[@class='book'][2]/descendant::*[position() = 4]` | | `<div>` element with class name `price` | `//div[@class='book'][2]/descendant::*[position() = 5]` | Even though the element is at the first position in the DOM, we have to start counting the position from the current node. We have to just remember that while using the `position()` function with XPath axes, the position is determined from the perspective of the current node. </Section> <Section> ### Summary - In Selenium, XPath axes are used to find elements in an HTML document based on their relationship to the current node. XPath axes provide a way to traverse the document structure relative to a particular context node. - The parent element of the current node refers to the immediate element that directly contains or wraps the current node in the DOM hierarchy. - The child elements are the immediate elements that are nested within and directly under the current node in the DOM hierarchy. - The XPath axis `parent` is used to select the parent element of the current node. - The XPath axis `child` is used to select the child elements of the current node. - The XPath axis `following-sibling` is used to identify and select the sibling elements that come after the current node. Siblings are at the same level as the current node and share its parent. - The XPath axis `preceding-sibling` is used to identify and select the sibling elements that come before the current node. - The XPath axis `descendant` is used to identify and select all descendant elements of the current node. - The XPath axis `ancestor` is used to identify and select all ancestor elements of the current node. - The XPath axis `following` is used to identify and select all elements that appear after the context node in the DOM hierarchy, excluding the current node, its descendants, and its ancestors. - The XPath axis `preceding` is used to identify and select all elements that appear before the context node in the DOM hierarchy, excluding the ancestor elements of the elements that come after the context node. - The XPath axis `ancestor-or-self` is used to identify and select the context node and all its ancestor elements in the DOM hierarchy. - The XPath axis `descendant-or-self` is used to identify and select the context node and all its descendant elements in the DOM hierarchy. </Section>

# CSS Selector Locator Part - 2
## Concepts CSS Selectors Combinator Selectors Child Selector Descendant Selector Adjacent Sibling Selector General Sibling Selector Test the Job Rating
## Introduction In the previous unit, we learned about the CSS Selector locator and we tested the Login and Home page functionality of the Jobby App by selecting web elements using CSS Simple Selectors and CSS Advanced Attribute Selectors. In this unit, we learn about CSS Combinator Selectors and we will test the job rating using combinator selectors. Click [here](https://new-assets.ccbp.in/frontend/content/qa-testing/JobbyAppTestCSS2.zip) to download the initial code for this project.
## 1. CSS Selectors We learned that CSS Selectors are one of the locator strategies offered by Selenium to identify web elements. CSS selectors primarily target elements based on their attributes, relationships with other elements, or specific element types. CSS selectors are similar to XPath with some advantages and disadvantages that we will discuss later. Selenium offers different types of CSS selectors that are categorized as - Simple Selectors - Advanced Attribute Selectors - Combinator Selectors - Pseudo-class Selectors We have learned how to use Simple Selectors and Advanced Attribute Selectors to locate the web elements. Now, we will learn about Combinator Selectors. ## 2. Combinator Selectors Similar to XPath Axes, CSS combinator Selectors are used to select elements based on their relationship to other elements There are four types of combinator selectors using which we find elements based on relationship: - Child Selector - Descendant Selector - Adjacent Sibling Selector - General Sibling Selector To identify an element based on relationship, we typically start by identifying a unique element on the web page and then use the combinator selectors to target elements nested/siblings of the unique element. So far, we have successfully tested the below functionalities: - Logging into the application - Navigating to the home page - Navigating to the jobs page and verifying the display of jobs Now, we are going to test the rating of the jobs on the jobs page of the Jobby application. Before we can test the rating of the job, we need to locate the element that contains the rating information. Let’s consider the sample Book Store application and understand how to locate elements using the combinator selectors. The link to the Book Store application is: https://qabookstore.ccbp.tech/. The tree representation of the "Book Store" DOM is as follows. We have a separate `
` tag for each book in the "Book Store" HTML DOM. Let's consider the `
` tag related to the "Harry Potter" book as the current node. Let's see the above `
` element in the DOM tree. We consider the second `
` element that is related to "Harry Potter" as the current node. We consider this `
` element as the current node throughout this unit. Let's learn about each combinator selector and use them to locate elements in our project. ### 2.1 Child Selector Child Selector is used to identify and select the child elements of the current node. Child elements are the immediate elements that are nested within and directly under the current node in the DOM hierarchy. #### Syntax In CSS Selector, we use `>` to select the child elements. Whereas in XPath, we use `/child::`. Let's see the child elements of our current node(`
` with `category` as `children`) in the DOM tree of "Book Store". Let's write the expression to select the child elements of the current node. The CSS selector expression would be, `div[category='children'] > *`. Here, - `div`: Selects all `
` elements anywhere in the DOM hierarchy. - `[category='children']`: Filters the selected `
` elements based on the condition that their `category` attribute value is 'children'. - `>*`: Selects the immediate elements that are nested within and directly under the current node in the DOM hierarchy. Similar to XPath expressions, we can also write CSS Selector expressions in the dev tools search bar: - Inspect the web page - Press Ctrl + F (or Cmd + F) to open the search bar However, there might be some limitations when it comes to using general selectors like the tag selector (\

). Eg: When we want to search for all p elements in the search bar, it will also match all the elements that have the letter "p" in their text such as ``, ``, etc. Let's select the child elements of our current node(`

` with `category` as `children`) in the HTML DOM tree of "Book Store". Let's learn another combinator selector, a descendant selector and understand how it can be used to locate the elements. ### 2.2 Descendant Selector Descendant Selector is used to identify and select the descendant elements of the current node. #### Syntax In CSS Selector, we use ` `(space) to select the descendant elements. Whereas in XPath, we use `/descendant::`. Let's see the descendant elements of our current node(`
` with `category` as `descendant`) in the DOM tree of "Book Store". Let's write the expression to select the descendant elements of the current node. The CSS selector expression would be, `div[category='children'] *`. Here, - `div`: Selects all `
` elements anywhere in the DOM hierarchy. - `[category='children']`: Filters the selected `
` elements based on the condition that their `category` attribute value is 'children'. - ` *`: Selects all descendant elements of the filtered `
` elements. Let's select the descendant elements of our current node(`
` with `category` as `descendant`) in the HTML DOM tree of "Book Store". Here, we can see that there are 5 descendant elements for the current node. Let's learn another combinator selector, adjacent sibling selector and understand how it can be used to locate the elements. ### 2.3 Adjacent Sibling Selector The adjacent sibling selector targets the sibling element that is right after the current element. It is used to select only one adjacent sibling element. #### Syntax ```xml element + * ``` Here, the `+` symbol is used to select the adjacent element of a specific element. The CSS expression that uses an adjacent sibling selector selects only the first element that comes after the div with category children. Let's see the adjacent sibling elements of our current node. Let's write the expression to select the adjacent sibling elements of the current node. The CSS selector expression would be, `div[category='children']+*`. Here, - `div`: Selects all `
` elements anywhere in the DOM hierarchy. - `[category='children']`: Filters the selected `
` elements based on the condition that their `category` attribute value is 'children'. - `+`: Selects the adjacent sibling elements of the filtered `
` elements. Let's select the adjacent sibling elements of our current node in the HTML DOM tree of "Book Store". Here, we can see that it selects only the first element that comes after the `
` with category `children`. Let's learn another combinator selector, the general sibling selector and understand how it can be used to locate the elements. ### 2.4 General Sibling Selector The general sibling selector is used to identify and select all the sibling elements that come after a specific element. Siblings are at the same level as the current node and share its parent. #### Syntax ```xml element ~ sibling element ``` Here, the `~` symbol is used to select the general sibling elements of a specific element. Let's see the general sibling elements of our current node. Let's write the expression to select the general sibling elements of the current node. The CSS selector expression would be, `div[category='children']~*`. Here, - `div`: Selects all `
` elements anywhere in the DOM hierarchy. - `[category='children']`: Filters the selected `
` elements based on the condition that their `category` attribute value is 'children'. - `~`: Selects all the sibling elements that come after a specific element. Let's select the general sibling elements of our current node in the HTML DOM tree of "Book Store". Here, we can see that it selects all the sibling elements(**2**) that comes after the `
` with category `children`. **XPath Axes vs CSS Combinators** | CSS combinator Selector | XPath Syntax | CSS Selector Syntax | | :---------------------: | :-------------------------: | :--------------------------: | | child | parentElement/child::* | parentElement > childElement | | descendant | parentElement/descendant::\* | parentElement \* | | adjacent-sibling | Doesn’t support | element + sibling element | | general-sibling | /following-sibling::* | element ~ sibling element | Here, XPath does not support adjacent sibling selectors. Therefore, we need to select the element by using suitable locators. A descendant selector must contain Space(' '), whereas other combinator selectors may not. We have learned about all the combinator selectors. Let's test the rating of the jobs on the jobs page of the Jobby application using these selectors.
## 3. Test the Job Rating Let’s locate the job rating using combinator selectors To test job rating functionality, we should first create the project and then we should write the tests for, - Login functionality - Navigating to the home page - Navigating to the jobs page - Verifying the display of jobs, etc. To avoid repeating the above steps every time, we can utilize the initial code provided in the [Introduction](#introduction) section. Extract the Downloaded Zip and open the project using IntelliJ. Update the "PATH_TO_CHROMEDRIVER" value in the `JobbyAppTest.java` file ### 3.1 Initial Code - Test Steps The initial code provides all the respective code to automate the below steps, 1. Launch Chrome Browser 2. Navigate to the login page 3. Enter the username and password 4. Click on the login button 5. User should be able to redirect to the home page 6. On the home page, locate and click on the "Find Jobs" button 7. User should be able to redirect to the Jobs Page 8. Validate the display of jobs Execute the initial code in the `JobbyAppTest.java` file. #### Output ``` Navigation to home page is successful! Navigation to jobs page is successful! Jobs are displayed successfully on the jobs page: 60 ``` To locate the job rating element, we must first locate the job uniquely and then locate the rating element. Let’s locate the job element using the href attribute of `` tag and then locate the rating element. The CSS selector expression to locate the job element would be, `a[href='/jobs/bb95e51b-b1b2-4d97-bee4-1d5ec2b96751']`. Now, we locate the child element using its tag name `li`. The CSS selector expression to locate the rating element would be, `a[href='/jobs/bb95e51b-b1b2-4d97-bee4-1d5ec2b96751'] > li`. Here, we can see that the rating element with `

` tag is the descendant element of the `

  • ` element we located. So, let's write the CSS selector expression to locate the rating element using its class attribute. The CSS selector expression to locate the rating element would be, `a[href='/jobs/bb95e51b-b1b2-4d97-bee4-1d5ec2b96751'] > li p.rating`. Here, we are using a descendant selector, we need to use Space(' ') after `li`. Now, we have located the rating element using the CSS selector expression. Let's use it in the code to test the rating functionality. Let's write the code to verify the job rating. ```java String expectedRating = "4"; WebElement jobRatingEle = driver.findElement(By.cssSelector("a[href='/jobs/bb95e51b-b1b2-4d97-bee4-1d5ec2b96751'] > li p.rating")); String rating = jobRatingEle.getText(); if(expectedRating.equals(rating)){ System.out.println("Rating is 4"); } else { System.out.println("Job Rating is not as expected"); } ``` Let's add the above code to our existing code so that it verifies the job rating only after all the jobs have been fully loaded. ```java import org.openqa.selenium.By; import org.openqa.selenium.WebDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.WebElement; import org.openqa.selenium.chrome.ChromeDriver; import org.openqa.selenium.support.ui.ExpectedConditions; import org.openqa.selenium.support.ui.WebDriverWait; import java.time.Duration; import java.util.List; public class JobbyAppTest { public static void main(String[] args) { // Set the path to the ChromeDriver executable System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "/home/nxtwavetech/Downloads/chromedriver_linux64/chromedriver"); // Open Chrome Browser WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(); // Navigate to the login page driver.get("https://qajobbyapp.ccbp.tech/login"); // Find and fill in the form fields WebElement usernameEl = driver.findElement(By.cssSelector("input#userNameInput")); usernameEl.sendKeys("rahul"); WebElement passwordEl = driver.findElement(By.cssSelector("input#passwordInput")); passwordEl.sendKeys("rahul@2021"); WebElement buttonEl = driver.findElement(By.cssSelector("button[type='submit']")); buttonEl.submit(); // Define the expected URL of the home page String homePageUrl = "https://qajobbyapp.ccbp.tech/"; // Wait for the expected URL to be loaded WebDriverWait wait = new WebDriverWait(driver, Duration.ofSeconds(10)); wait.until(ExpectedConditions.urlToBe(homePageUrl)); // Get the current URL and verify redirection to home page String currentUrl = driver.getCurrentUrl(); if (currentUrl.equals(homePageUrl)) { System.out.println("Navigation to home page is successful!"); } // Find and click on the "Find Jobs" button WebElement findJobsButtonEl = driver.findElement(By.cssSelector("button.find-jobs-button")); findJobsButtonEl.click(); // Define the expected URL of the home page String jobsPageUrl = "https://qajobbyapp.ccbp.tech/jobs"; // Wait for the expected URL to be loaded wait.until(ExpectedConditions.urlToBe(jobsPageUrl)); // Get the current URL and verify redirection to jobs page currentUrl = driver.getCurrentUrl(); if (currentUrl.equals(jobsPageUrl)) { System.out.println("Navigation to jobs page is successful!"); } wait.until(ExpectedConditions.visibilityOfElementLocated(By.cssSelector("ul.jobs-list"))); // Verify the display of jobs on the jobs page List jobs = driver.findElements(By.cssSelector("li[class *= 'job-it']")); if (jobs.size() > 0) { System.out.println("Jobs are displayed successfully on the jobs page: " + jobs.size()); String expectedRating = "4"; WebElement jobRatingEle = driver.findElement(By.cssSelector("a[href='/jobs/bb95e51b-b1b2-4d97-bee4-1d5ec2b96751'] > li p.rating")); String rating = jobRatingEle.getText(); if (expectedRating.equals(rating)) { System.out.println("Rating is 4"); } else { System.out.println("Job Rating is not as expected"); } } else { System.out.println("No Jobs found on the jobs page."); } // Close the browser driver.quit(); } } ``` Let's run the above code to check the output. #### Output ``` Navigation to home page is successful! Navigation to jobs page is successful! Jobs are displayed successfully on the jobs page: 60 Rating is 4 ``` Hurray! We have successfully tested the job rating functionality using CSS combinator selectors. Let's see the difference between the XPath and CSS selectors. **XPath vs CSS Selectors** In CSS selectors, the flow of finding the elements is always a one-way direction not a two-way direction i.e., we cannot find the parent, or ancestor element from the child element. We will learn about the Psueo-class selectors in the next section.
    • ### Summary - Similar to XPath Axes, CSS combinator Selectors are used to select elements based on their relationship to other elements There are four types of combinator selectors using which we find elements based on relationship: - Child Selector - Descendant Selector - Adjacent Sibling Selector - General Sibling SelectorBe - Child Selector is used to identify and select the child elements of the current node. - In CSS Selector, we use the `>` to select the child elements. Whereas in XPath, we use `/child::`. - Descendant Selector is used to identify and select the descendant elements of the current node. - In CSS Selector, we use the ` `(space) to select the descendant elements. Whereas in XPath, we use `/descendant::`. - The adjacent sibling selector targets the sibling element that is right after the current element. It is used to select only one adjacent sibling element. - In CSS Selector, we use the `+` symbol to select the adjacent sibling element of a specific element. - The general sibling selector is used to identify and select all the sibling elements that come after a specific element. - In CSS Selector, we use the `~` symbol to select the general sibling element of a specific element.
